set-01-A-001.revisionNote: Statements D and E reworded by DOMiNANCE so that each has a definite answer; the originals depended on unstated conditions.
set-01-A-001.originalExplanation:
A False: in early systole the contracting left ventricle compresses its intramural vessels, so left coronary inflow is at its lowest; most LV flow occurs in diastole.
B True: hypoxia releases adenosine, K+, CO₂ and H+, which dilate coronary arterioles (metabolic regulation is the main control of coronary flow).
C False: hypothermia lowers myocardial metabolism and oxygen demand, so coronary flow falls.
D True: direct α-adrenergic effects mildly constrict coronary vessels, but the rise in heart rate and contractility raises O₂ demand, and metabolic vasodilation wins, so flow increases.
E False: autoregulation adjusts coronary resistance so flow stays nearly constant across the autoregulatory range (about 60-140 mmHg).

set-01-A-002.originalExplanation:
A False: at rest most ventricular filling is passive; atrial contraction adds only about 20-30% at the end of diastole (more at high heart rates).
B False: during isovolumetric relaxation both AV and semilunar valves are closed, so no filling occurs; filling starts when the AV valves open.
C True: a third heart sound comes from rapid early filling vibrating the ventricular wall and can be normal in children, young adults, athletes and pregnancy.
D False: filling depends on atrial pressure exceeding ventricular pressure, not on atmospheric pressure.
E True: the rapid filling phase in early diastole delivers most of the filling volume; later filling (diastasis) is slow.

set-01-A-003.originalExplanation:
A False: the left atrial wall is only slightly thicker than the right; the threefold difference applies to the ventricles (LV vs RV).
B False: excitation starts at the SA node in the right atrium, so the right atrium is activated first.
C False: the fibrous skeleton insulates atria from ventricles; the only normal electrical path is the AV node and bundle of His.
D False: atrial systole comes first (about 0.1-0.2 s before ventricular systole), giving the AV nodal delay time for atria to top up the ventricles.
E True: as the ventricles contract, the base (AV ring) is pulled down towards the apex, shortening the long axis of the ventricles.

set-01-A-004.originalExplanation:
A True: arteriolar dilation transmits more arterial pressure to the capillaries, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration.
B True: on standing, the column of blood adds gravitational pressure to leg capillaries, increasing filtration (hence ankle swelling).
C False: lymphatic obstruction causes oedema by stopping drainage of filtered fluid. It does not increase filtration; the rising interstitial pressure actually reduces it.
D True: venous obstruction raises venous and therefore capillary hydrostatic pressure.
E True: low plasma albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so less fluid is held in the capillaries and net filtration increases.

set-01-A-005.originalExplanation:
A False: Korotkoff sounds are made by turbulent blood flow and arterial wall vibration in the partly compressed brachial artery, not by the heart.
B True: the first tapping sounds (phase I) appear when cuff pressure falls just below systolic pressure and blood starts to spurt through.
C False: diastolic pressure is taken at the disappearance of sounds (phase V), or muffling (phase IV) in some cases, not at the loudest sounds.
D False: the palpatory method usually reads lower, because a pulse can be felt only a little after flow restarts; auscultatory systolic readings tend to be higher.
E True: the bladder must encircle about 80% of the arm; a cuff too small for a large arm falsely raises the reading.

set-01-A-006.originalExplanation:
A False: by Poiseuille's law resistance is proportional to 1/r^4, so halving the radius increases resistance 16-fold, not by 50%.
B False: resistance depends on lumen radius, vessel length and viscosity; wall thickness is not in the equation (it matters only if it narrows the lumen).
C True: vascular smooth-muscle tone sets the lumen radius, especially in arterioles, so contraction raises resistance.
D True: resistance is directly proportional to viscosity, so polycythaemia raises it and anaemia lowers it.
E False: arterioles are the main site of resistance; capillaries are individually narrow but lie in huge numbers in parallel, so the capillary bed's total resistance is lower.

set-01-A-007.originalExplanation:
A True: exercise raises sympathetic outflow to increase heart rate and contractility.
B True: excitement and arousal (fight-or-flight) increase sympathetic drive.
C True: hypotension reduces baroreceptor firing, which disinhibits the vasomotor centre and increases sympathetic outflow.
D True: emotional inputs from the limbic system and hypothalamus excite the pressor area of the medullary vasomotor centre.
E False: a sudden rise in blood pressure increases baroreceptor firing, which reduces sympathetic drive and increases vagal tone (the baroreceptor reflex), slowing the heart.

set-01-A-008.revisionNote: Statement D reworded by DOMiNANCE. The original referred to a non-standard 'RT interval'; QT is the recognised measure.
set-01-A-008.originalExplanation:
A False: electrical events come before mechanical ones; the QRS complex comes just before ventricular contraction.
B True: the T wave represents ventricular repolarisation.
C False: the P wave is atrial depolarisation; the PR interval spans atrial depolarisation plus conduction through the AV node and His-Purkinje system.
D True: the QT interval (QRS onset to T-wave end) is ventricular electrical systole, which roughly matches the ventricular action-potential duration; it shortens as heart rate rises, hence the corrected QTc.
E True: R-R intervals shorten in inspiration and lengthen in expiration (sinus arrhythmia), reflecting changes in vagal tone.

set-01-A-009.revisionNote: Statement A reworded by DOMiNANCE to state the condition (constant velocity); the original answer depended on it.
set-01-A-009.originalExplanation:
Turbulence is predicted by Reynolds number, Re = density × velocity × diameter / viscosity; a higher Re means more turbulence.
A False: at constant velocity a smaller diameter LOWERS Re. (At a stenosis velocity rises, so local turbulence can increase, but velocity is held constant here.)
B False: lower density lowers Re.
C False: lower velocity lowers Re.
D True: viscosity is in the denominator, so lower viscosity raises Re.
E True: anaemia lowers viscosity and raises cardiac output (velocity), so turbulence and flow murmurs become more likely.

set-01-A-010.originalExplanation:
The Fick principle gives CO = O2 uptake / (arterial O2 content - mixed venous O2 content).
A True: it measures the blood flow through the lungs, which equals cardiac output when there are no shunts.
B False: O2 CONTENTS (mL O2 per L blood) are used, not partial pressures; PO2 alone ignores haemoglobin-bound oxygen.
C False: whole-body O2 uptake is measured from inspired and expired gas volumes and concentrations (spirometry), not from alveolar PO2.
D True: properly mixed venous blood is sampled from the pulmonary artery via a catheter.
E True: pulmonary venous blood has the same O2 content as systemic arterial blood; in practice any systemic artery is sampled instead.

set-01-B-001.originalExplanation:
The Frank-Starling (length-tension) relationship states that, within physiological limits, the more a muscle is stretched before it contracts, the greater the tension it generates. In the heart, greater end-diastolic volume gives a stronger contraction.
Not A: Ca2+ release determines contractility (inotropy), which is separate from length.
Not B: the relation is not exponential; tension peaks at optimal length and falls with overstretch.
Not D: coronary perfusion is not the stretch stimulus.
Not E: greater load (afterload) actually reduces shortening.

set-01-B-002.originalExplanation:
Blood flows silently (laminar) through an open artery. When the cuff partly compresses the artery, blood spurts through the narrowing at high velocity and becomes turbulent, producing the Korotkoff sounds heard with the stethoscope.
Not B: normal laminar arterial flow does not make audible sounds.
Not C: there are no sounds to accentuate; the cuff creates them.
Not D: wall vibration happens, but it is driven by turbulent flow through the narrowing.
Not E: turbulence explains the method.

set-01-B-003.originalExplanation:
The SA node has intrinsic automaticity, so a denervated heart (e.g. after transplant) still beats, at about 90-100 beats/min, and supports life.
Not A: nerves modulate the heartbeat but do not start it.
Not C: rate can still change through circulating adrenaline, temperature and stretch of the SA node.
Not D: losing autonomic control reduces the speed of adaptation, so the heart is not more efficient.
Not E: valves still close and make heart sounds.

set-01-B-004.originalExplanation:
Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute, into either the pulmonary circulation (RV) or the systemic circulation (LV); both outputs are normally almost equal (about 5 L/min at rest).
Not A: work per minute is cardiac power, not volume.
Not C: bleeding from a cut aorta reflects collapsing pressure and resistance, not normal output.
Not D: cardiac output applies at rest as well as in exercise.
Not E: B is correct.

set-01-B-005.originalExplanation:
Just after LV systole starts, ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure (mitral valve closes, S1) but has not yet exceeded aortic pressure (aortic valve still closed). This is isovolumetric contraction, with both valves closed.
Not A: both are open at no point in a normal cycle.
Not C: an open mitral and closed aortic valve describes diastolic filling.
Not D: valve states depend on pressure gradients, not on sympathetic activity.
Not E: B is correct.

set-01-B-006.originalExplanation:
Gap junctions (connexin channels) let ionic current pass directly between neighbouring myocytes, so depolarisation spreads quickly and the ventricle behaves as a functional syncytium.
Not B: intercalated discs are the larger structures that contain gap junctions plus desmosomes; the specific conducting element is the gap junction.
Not C: mitochondria supply ATP.
Not D: the Golgi apparatus processes proteins.
Not E: SR calcium drives contraction, not the spread of depolarisation.

set-01-B-007.originalExplanation:
Endothelin-1, released by the endothelium, is a potent vasoconstrictor (via ETA receptors on smooth muscle), so more endothelin reduces arteriolar flow.
Not A: high pCO2 is a metabolic vasodilator.
Not B: a fall in pH (acidosis) dilates arterioles.
Not C: heat dilates vessels (e.g. in active tissue and skin).
Not E: nitric oxide relaxes smooth muscle through cGMP.

set-01-B-008.originalExplanation:
Capillary hydrostatic pressure is the main force pushing fluid OUT of capillaries, so it promotes filtration rather than opposing it.
Not A: plasma oncotic pressure (mainly albumin) pulls fluid back into capillaries.
Not B: a positive tissue fluid (interstitial hydrostatic) pressure pushes against filtration.
Not D: in this question's Starling framework, lymphatic and tissue-side pressure is counted as opposing filtration.
Not E: C is clearly an exception.

set-01-B-009.revisionNote: Rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original had two options labelled A and an ambiguous 'A and B' option, and 'seat of emotions' made the answer obvious.
set-01-B-009.originalExplanation:
The main blood reservoir is the systemic VEINS (about 60-70% of blood volume), not the heart, which holds only about 7%.
Not A: atrial myocytes secrete ANP, which promotes Na+ and water excretion.
Not B: ventricular contraction creates the pressure gradient that drives flow around both circulations.
Not C: the septa and valves keep the pulmonary (deoxygenated) and systemic (oxygenated) streams apart.
Not E: atrial volume (low-pressure) receptors sense filling and trigger ANP release and the Bainbridge and volume reflexes.

set-01-B-010.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE so that only one statement is true. The original item had more than one correct answer (A, C and D).
set-01-B-010.originalExplanation:
Low alveolar PO₂ causes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which sends blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli towards well-ventilated ones and so matches perfusion to ventilation.
Not A: pulmonary arteries carry DEoxygenated blood to the lungs; the pulmonary veins carry the freshly oxygenated blood.
Not B: the heart extracts about 70-75% of the O₂ delivered to it, so coronary sinus blood has the LOWEST O₂ content in the body, below mixed venous blood.
Not C: aortic flow is slightly MORE, because bronchial and Thebesian venous blood drains into the left heart (a small physiological shunt).
Not E: hypoxia DILATES systemic arterioles (metabolic vasodilation). This is the opposite of the pulmonary response, which is why D and E make a useful contrast.

set-01-B-011.originalExplanation:
All the listed tissues generate measurable electrical activity: SA and AV nodal cells produce slow-response (pacemaker) action potentials; working myocytes and His-bundle fibres produce fast-response action potentials. Their summed activity is what the ECG records.
Not A to D: each produces action potentials, so none is an exception. E is therefore correct.

set-01-B-012.originalExplanation:
Cardiac muscle has no motor units: it works as a functional syncytium in which every cell contracts with each beat. Its strength is graded by preload and contractility, not by recruitment, so A is false.
Not B: the Frank-Starling mechanism means a larger end-diastolic volume gives a larger stroke volume.
Not C: more or longer SR Ca2+ release increases force.
Not D: positive inotropes by definition raise contractility.
Not E: adrenaline acts on beta1 receptors to increase Ca2+ entry and contractility.

set-01-B-013.originalExplanation:
Capillaries are arranged in vast numbers in parallel, so their combined cross-sectional area is huge (about 1000 times that of the aorta). Resistances in parallel add as reciprocals, so total resistance stays low and flow velocity is slow, which helps exchange.
Not A: capillaries do lack valves, but that does not explain low resistance.
Not C: vessels in series add resistance.
Not D: precapillary sphincters open and close at different times, not all together.
Not E: the whole cardiac output passes through the capillaries.

set-01-B-014.originalExplanation: Capillaries are about 5-8 micrometres wide, about the same as or smaller than a red cell (about 7.5 micrometres). Red cells pass in single file and often deform to squeeze through, which shortens the diffusion distance for oxygen. Two or more cells side by side would need a lumen at least twice as wide, so B to E are wrong.

set-01-B-015.originalExplanation:
Lymphatic capillaries begin as blind-ended tubes in the interstitium. Their overlapping endothelial cells act as one-way flaps that let interstitial fluid and protein in.
Not A: blood capillaries connect arterioles to venules and are open at both ends.
Not B: sinusoids are wide, leaky capillaries (e.g. in the liver) that are also continuous with the circulation.
Not C: venules drain capillaries.
Not E: coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses.

set-01-B-016.originalExplanation:
Mitral stenosis narrows the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle, so blood flows slowly into the LV throughout diastole and filling is delayed and reduced.
Not A: aortic stenosis mainly obstructs ejection.
Not B: tricuspid regurgitation is a right-sided valve leak.
Not D: pulmonary stenosis obstructs right ventricular outflow.
Not E: a rise from 80 to 100 beats/min shortens diastole only slightly and does not significantly impair LV filling.

set-01-B-017.originalExplanation:
The Frank-Starling mechanism matches the two ventricles beat by beat. If the RV briefly pumps more, pulmonary venous return to the LV increases, LV end-diastolic volume rises and LV stroke volume increases until the outputs match again.
Not A, B, C: sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves and adrenaline act on both ventricles together; they change overall output but do not balance the ventricles against each other.
Not E: only D does the balancing.

set-01-B-018.originalExplanation:
In rapid ejection the aortic valve is open and blood enters the aorta faster than it runs off into the periphery, so aortic pressure rises to its systolic peak.
Not A: the mitral valve is closed throughout systole.
Not C: the aortic valve must be open for ejection.
Not D: ventricular volume is lowest at the END of ejection (end-systolic volume), not during rapid ejection.
Not E: S1 (AV valve closure) marks the start of isovolumetric contraction, before ejection.

set-01-B-019.originalExplanation:
Protein in the interstitium raises interstitial oncotic pressure, which reduces the net oncotic gradient that normally pulls fluid back into capillaries. Filtration therefore INCREASES, so a decrease in filtration is the exception.
Not A: lymph flow rises to remove the extra fluid and protein.
Not B: interstitial oncotic pressure goes up.
Not D: if drainage cannot keep up, oedema forms.
Not E: the plasma-minus-interstitial oncotic gradient decreases.

set-01-B-020.originalExplanation:
The RV starts ejecting first. The pulmonary artery diastolic pressure (about 8-10 mmHg) is far lower than aortic diastolic pressure (about 80 mmHg), so the RV opens its outflow valve sooner, even though LV contraction begins slightly earlier.
Not A: the LV has a much thicker wall and greater muscle mass.
Not B: depolarisation begins on the left side of the septum and LV activation slightly leads.
Not C: the LV generates about 120 mmHg against about 25 mmHg in the RV.
Not D: same stroke volume at higher pressure means more work.

set-02-A-001.originalExplanation:
By Poiseuille's law, resistance is proportional to 1/r^4. Doubling the diameter doubles the radius, so resistance becomes 1/2^4 = 1/16 of its original value.
Not A: 1/2 would apply only if resistance were proportional to 1/r.
Not C or D: resistance falls, not rises, when a tube widens.
Not E: radius is the most powerful determinant of resistance.

set-02-A-002.originalExplanation:
Korotkoff sounds come from turbulent, intermittent spurts of blood through the partly compressed artery. When cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure, the artery stays open throughout the cycle, flow becomes continuous and laminar, and the sounds muffle and then disappear (diastolic point).
Not A: intermittent flow is what CREATES turbulence.
Not B: AV valve opening is a cardiac event and is not heard at the cuff.
Not C: the patient's blood pressure has not changed; only cuff pressure has.
Not E: systolic pressure marks the START of the sounds.

set-02-A-003.originalExplanation:
Fick principle: cardiac output = whole-body O2 consumption / (arterial O2 content - mixed venous O2 content). These three values are all you need.
Not B: CO2 values can be used in a variant method but are not required.
Not C: cardiac O2 consumption and coronary sinus O2 give coronary blood flow, not cardiac output.
Not D: both ventricles pump the same output, so no split is needed.
Not E: gender is irrelevant to the calculation.

set-02-A-004.originalExplanation:
Losing a third of blood volume reduces venous return, stroke volume and arterial pressure. Less stretch of the carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors reduces their firing, so the medulla withdraws vagal tone and increases sympathetic outflow, raising heart rate (and constricting vessels).
Not A: a smaller volume does not directly drive the SA node; the reflex does.
Not B: vagal activity decreases.
Not D: sympathetic outflow to muscle vessels is mainly vasoconstrictor here, not cholinergic dilator.
Not E: vagal activity falls.

set-02-A-005.originalExplanation:
Contractility (inotropy) is the strength of contraction independent of preload and heart rate. If output rises with heart rate and LV end-diastolic pressure (a preload index) unchanged, stroke volume must have risen through stronger contraction, i.e. higher contractility.
Not B: that is a chronotropic effect.
Not C: that is the Frank-Starling (preload) effect.
Not D: increased contractility shifts the curve up and to the LEFT (more force at the same length).
Not E: A is correct.

set-02-A-006.originalExplanation:
Oxygen is carried mainly (about 98%) bound to haemoglobin inside red cells; only about 1.5-2% is dissolved in plasma, so O2 transport is not primarily a plasma function.
Not A: hormones travel in plasma, free or bound to carrier proteins.
Not B: plasma osmolality and protein keep red cells at normal size.
Not C: chylomicrons are carried in plasma (lymph then blood).
Not D: antibodies (immunoglobulins) are plasma proteins.

set-02-A-007.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original had no correct option, because its 'red and white cells and platelets' answer included the buffy coat.
set-02-A-007.originalExplanation:
Haematocrit (packed cell volume) is the fraction of whole-blood volume taken up by red cells after centrifugation, normally about 40-54% in men and 36-48% in women.
Not A: haemoglobin is almost entirely inside red cells.
Not B: plasma would be about 59% of this sample.
Not D: red cells make up over 99% of formed elements, so the fraction of formed elements is not 41%; the denominator must be whole blood.
Not E: plasma proteins are only about 7 g/dL; haematocrit has nothing to do with them.

set-02-A-008.originalExplanation:
The heartbeat is myogenic: it starts spontaneously in the SA node, not in a nerve. Nerves only change the rate and force. So A is the false statement.
Not B: impulses pass cell to cell through gap junctions.
Not C: pacemaker cells (SA, AV nodes) have unstable membrane potentials that drift towards threshold.
Not D: working atrial and ventricular myocytes have stable resting potentials (about -90 mV).
Not E: the long refractory period makes ventricles inexcitable for most of systole, which prevents tetany.

set-02-A-009.originalExplanation:
The SA node has the fastest spontaneous depolarisation (phase 4 slope from the funny current If and Ca2+ currents), so it reaches threshold first and drives slower pacemakers (overdrive suppression).
Not A: innervation modulates rate but does not explain pacemaker status.
Not B: AV node, His and Purkinje cells can also generate action potentials.
Not D: SA nodal cells have the LEAST stable potential.
Not E: the SA node is highly sensitive to catecholamines.

set-02-A-010.originalExplanation:
When P waves and QRS complexes have no fixed relationship (AV dissociation), atrial impulses are not reaching the ventricles. This is complete (third-degree) heart block from failure of AV conduction, and the ventricles are driven by an escape pacemaker.
Not A: early repolarisation changes the ST segment.
Not C: SA depression slows or removes P waves but keeps P-QRS linkage.
Not D: slowed AV conduction lengthens the PR interval (first-degree block) but every P is still followed by a QRS.
Not E: LBBB widens the QRS but P-QRS linkage is kept.

set-02-A-011.revisionNote: Option E corrected by DOMiNANCE. The original compared the left ventricle with itself, an apparent typo.
set-02-A-011.originalExplanation:
Frank-Starling law: greater end-diastolic volume stretches the fibres towards optimal overlap and increases troponin's Ca2+ sensitivity, so the heart contracts more strongly and stroke volume rises.
Not B: cardiac output rises with stroke volume.
Not C: higher end-diastolic volumes usually go with higher, not lower, venous pressure.
Not D: contraction force increases.
Not E: when filling rises in both ventricles, the Frank-Starling mechanism keeps the two outputs matched; neither ventricle persistently out-pumps the other.

set-02-A-012.originalExplanation:
Initial fibre length (preload, set by end-diastolic volume) is a major determinant of contractile force through the Frank-Starling mechanism; the other major factor is contractility.
Not B or C: intercalated discs and gap junctions allow electrical coupling, and their number does not vary beat to beat to control force.
Not D: SA nodal depolarisation sets rate, not force.
Not E: His bundle length is fixed and only affects conduction.

set-02-A-013.originalExplanation:
Inotropy refers to the force of contraction, so a positive inotrope increases contractility, e.g. adrenaline, digoxin or dobutamine.
Not A: higher contractility usually increases stroke volume.
Not B: that describes diffusion or chemotaxis.
Not C: SA node rate effects are chronotropic.
Not E: end-diastolic volume reflects preload, not inotropy.

set-02-A-014.originalExplanation:
Higher carotid sinus pressure stretches the baroreceptors and increases their firing. The medulla responds by lowering sympathetic outflow and increasing vagal tone, causing bradycardia, arteriolar dilation and a fall in pressure. Atrial tachycardia is the opposite of this response, so E is the exception.
Not A: sympathetic tone falls.
Not B: aortic pressure falls.
Not C: vagal activity causes reflex bradycardia.
Not D: withdrawal of sympathetic constrictor tone dilates arterioles.

set-02-A-015.originalExplanation:
Vagal acetylcholine acts on M2 receptors, opening K+ channels (IK-ACh) and reducing If and Ca2+ currents. This slows SA node firing and so slows the heart.
Not B: SA node activity decreases.
Not C: AV nodal conduction slows (negative dromotropy).
Not D: there is little vagal supply to the ventricles; atrial force falls slightly, but ventricular force is not increased.
Not E: only A is correct.

set-02-A-016.originalExplanation:
In active muscle, local metabolites (adenosine, K+, H+, CO2, lactate, low O2, raised osmolality) dilate arterioles, overriding sympathetic constriction (functional sympatholysis) and keeping flow high in step with demand.
Not A: aortic pressure rises only modestly and would be useless without local dilation.
Not B: alpha-adrenergic impulses constrict.
Not C: beta2 dilation from adrenaline helps a little but is not the main mechanism.
Not D: splanchnic and renal constriction redirects some flow but does not open muscle vessels.

set-02-A-017.originalExplanation:
Tissue blood flow is mainly matched to metabolic demand: metabolites from active tissue (adenosine, CO2, H+, K+, low O2) dilate local arterioles, a process called metabolic autoregulation or active hyperaemia.
Not A: transmural pressure contributes to myogenic autoregulation but is secondary.
Not C or D: nerves and hormones mainly serve whole-body pressure control.
Not E: cardiac output sets the total supply, not how it is shared among tissues.

set-02-A-018.originalExplanation:
The P wave is atrial muscle depolarisation. Atrial muscle is a large enough mass to produce a signal visible at the body surface.
Not A: the SA node is too small to be seen on the surface ECG; it is 'silent' before the P wave.
Not B: AV nodal conduction is hidden within the PR segment.
Not C: His bundle activity needs an intracardiac (His bundle) electrogram.
Not D: Bachmann's bundle is a small interatrial pathway that is not seen separately.

set-02-A-019.originalExplanation:
With stroke volume and arterial compliance constant, pulse pressure (roughly stroke volume / compliance) stays about the same, so it is the exception. A slower rate lowers cardiac output (HR x SV), which lowers mean arterial pressure (CO x TPR). The whole pressure wave shifts down, so systolic and diastolic pressures both fall, and diastolic falls further with the longer diastolic run-off.
Not A, B, C, E: each decreases. In real circulations pulse pressure can change slightly with rate.

set-02-A-020.originalExplanation:
No P waves with normal, narrow QRS complexes means the ventricles are activated normally through the His-Purkinje system from above, but the atria are not driving them. This is a junctional (AV nodal) rhythm, usually at 40-60 beats/min; retrograde P waves may be hidden in the QRS.
Not A: SA node rhythm produces visible P waves.
Not C: a His bundle focus is possible but less common.
Not D or E: Purkinje or ventricular foci produce wide, bizarre QRS complexes.

set-02-A-021.originalExplanation:
Increased contractility means the ventricle ejects more blood from the same starting (end-diastolic) volume, i.e. greater stroke volume and output for a given preload.
Not A or C: end-systolic volume is an OUTCOME of ejection, not a fixed reference; higher contractility actually lowers it.
Not D: that describes decreased contractility.
Not E: refractoriness is unrelated to contractility.

set-02-A-022.originalExplanation:
During the PR interval the atria depolarise and the impulse passes through the AV node and His-Purkinje system, but ventricular muscle is not yet activated.
Not A: the QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation.
Not B: the QT interval spans ventricular depolarisation through repolarisation.
Not C: in the ST segment the ventricles are fully depolarised (plateau phase), which is why it is normally isoelectric.

set-02-A-023.originalExplanation:
Raised venous pressure is transmitted back to the capillaries, increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration, e.g. ankle oedema in right heart failure.
Not A: arteriolar constriction lowers capillary pressure and reduces filtration.
Not C: more plasma protein raises plasma oncotic pressure, pulling fluid back in.
Not D: dehydration reduces blood volume and concentrates plasma proteins, both of which reduce filtration.

set-02-A-024.originalExplanation:
Contraction is triggered by Ca2+ binding to troponin C, which uncovers myosin-binding sites on actin. The amount of free cytosolic Ca2+ during systole is the main determinant of contractile force; inotropes such as adrenaline and digoxin work by increasing it.
Not A: Na+ affects contractility only indirectly via Na+/Ca2+ exchange.
Not B: K+ sets resting potential.
Not D: Cl- has little direct role.
Not E: Mg2+ is not the controlling ion.

set-02-A-025.originalExplanation:
The two ventricles are in series, so over time they must pump the same volume per minute (100%); otherwise blood would build up in one circulation. Small beat-to-beat differences are corrected by the Frank-Starling mechanism.
Not A, B, C: lower percentages would quickly cause systemic congestion.
Not E: a higher percentage would flood the lungs and cause pulmonary oedema.

set-02-A-026.originalExplanation:
Cardiovascular reflexes, mainly the baroreceptor reflex, are organised to keep arterial blood pressure fairly constant. Steady pressure lets each tissue regulate its own flow by adjusting local resistance.
Not A: oxygen delivery is matched locally, not held constant.
Not B: arteriolar resistance changes widely by design.
Not D: cardiac output varies greatly (e.g. 5 to 25 L/min in exercise) while pressure is defended.

set-02-A-027.originalExplanation:
The AV nodal delay (about 0.1 s) lets the atria contract and finish filling the ventricles before ventricular systole begins. It also limits how many fast atrial impulses reach the ventricles.
Not A: aortic run-off occurs throughout diastole regardless.
Not B: venous return to the atria happens continuously.
Not D: ventricular contraction follows the delay rather than happening during it.
Not E: ventricular repolarisation occurs later (T wave).

set-02-A-028.originalExplanation:
Preload is the stretch on ventricular fibres before contraction, which is most directly reflected by LV end-diastolic volume.
Not A: blood volume is a distant determinant.
Not B: central venous pressure reflects right-sided filling and depends on venous compliance.
Not C: wedge pressure estimates left atrial pressure, which is one step removed.
Not E: LV end-diastolic pressure depends on ventricular compliance as well as volume, so a stiff ventricle shows high pressure with low volume.

set-02-A-029.originalExplanation:
Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, increasing venous return to the right heart; RV ejection lasts longer and pulmonary vascular capacitance rises, so the pulmonary valve closes later (P2 delayed). Left-sided return falls slightly, so A2 comes a little earlier, widening the split.
Not A: aortic closure occurs slightly EARLIER.
Not B: mitral opening does not create S2.
Not D: LV stroke volume falls slightly in inspiration.
Not E: heart rate usually rises in inspiration (sinus arrhythmia).

set-02-A-030.originalExplanation:
Anaemia lowers blood viscosity (less resistance and more venous return) and reduces tissue oxygen delivery, causing local vasodilation and sympathetic activation. Cardiac output stays high (a high-output state).
Not A: in established hypertension cardiac output is usually normal and resistance is raised.
Not B: aortic stenosis limits output.
Not D: complete heart block gives a slow escape rate and low output.
Not E: tamponade restricts filling and lowers output.

set-02-A-031.originalExplanation:
Raised intracranial pressure compresses cerebral vessels, causing brainstem ischaemia, which triggers strong sympathetic vasoconstriction and raises blood pressure. Baroreceptors then cause reflex bradycardia (the Cushing reflex, often with irregular breathing).
Not A: exercise raises both pressure and heart rate.
Not B: fever raises heart rate and causes skin vasodilation.
Not C: altitude hypoxia increases heart rate.
Not E: haemorrhage lowers pressure and raises heart rate.

set-02-A-032.originalExplanation:
Increased postcapillary (venular) resistance holds back blood leaving the capillaries, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and therefore net filtration.
Not A: precapillary sphincter contraction lowers capillary pressure.
Not B: lower arterial pressure reduces capillary pressure.
Not C: higher plasma protein raises oncotic pressure, which opposes filtration.
Not D: lower permeability reduces the filtration coefficient.

set-02-A-033.originalExplanation:
Veins and venules are thin-walled and highly compliant capacitance vessels holding about 60-70% of blood volume, which can be mobilised by venoconstriction.
Not A: the heart holds about 7%.
Not B or C: the aorta, arteries and arterioles together hold about 10-15%.
Not D: capillaries hold only about 5% at any moment, despite their huge number.

set-02-A-034.originalExplanation:
Reynolds number (Re = density x velocity x diameter / viscosity) predicts turbulence; flow tends to become turbulent when Re exceeds about 2000. Higher velocity raises Re, e.g. across stenosed valves (murmurs) or in high-output states.
Not B: higher viscosity lowers Re.
Not C: a smaller diameter lowers Re at the same velocity.
Not D: lower density lowers Re.
Not E: vessel length is not part of Reynolds number.

set-02-A-035.originalExplanation:
Arrhythmia (dysrhythmia) means any abnormal rate, rhythm or conduction pattern of the heart; the core feature in this option set is irregular rhythm.
Not A: rapid contraction alone is tachycardia, which may still be regular.
Not C or D: valve disorders are structural and are not arrhythmias in themselves.
Not E: a regular beat is normal rhythm.

set-02-A-036.originalExplanation:
By the time blood reaches the veins, arterial pulsations have been damped out by the compliant arteries and high-resistance arterioles, so venous flow is steady and smooth (non-pulsatile).
Not A: veins normally show no arterial-type pulse (except jugular waves from the right atrium).
Not C: systemic veins carry deoxygenated blood away from tissues.
Not D: venous velocity is generally lower than arterial.
Not E: venous valves ensure one-way flow.

set-02-A-037.originalExplanation:
The pulmonary and systemic circulations are in series, so pulmonary blood flow equals systemic blood flow (cardiac output).
Not B: pulmonary vascular resistance is about one-tenth of systemic resistance, which is why pulmonary pressures are low.
Not C: pulmonary veins carry freshly oxygenated blood with LOW CO2.
Not D: pulmonary hypertension overloads the RIGHT ventricle (cor pulmonale).
Not E: pulmonary veins drain into the LEFT atrium.

set-02-A-038.originalExplanation:
The SA node has intrinsic automaticity, so a denervated heart (e.g. after transplant) still beats, at about 90-100 beats/min, and supports life.
Not A: nerves modulate the heartbeat but do not start it.
Not C: rate can still change through circulating adrenaline, temperature and stretch of the SA node.
Not D: losing autonomic control reduces the speed of adaptation, so the heart is not more efficient.
Not E: valves still close and make heart sounds.

set-02-A-039.originalExplanation:
Just after LV systole starts, ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure (mitral valve closes, S1) but has not yet exceeded aortic pressure (aortic valve still closed). This is isovolumetric contraction, with both valves closed.
Not A: both are open at no point in a normal cycle.
Not C: an open mitral and closed aortic valve describes diastolic filling.
Not D: valve states depend on pressure gradients, not on sympathetic activity.
Not E: B is correct.

set-02-A-040.originalExplanation:
Gap junctions (connexin channels) let ionic current pass directly between neighbouring myocytes, so depolarisation spreads quickly and the ventricle behaves as a functional syncytium.
Not B: intercalated discs are the larger structures that contain gap junctions plus desmosomes; the specific conducting element is the gap junction.
Not C: mitochondria supply ATP.
Not D: the Golgi apparatus processes proteins.
Not E: SR calcium drives contraction, not the spread of depolarisation.

set-03-A-001.originalExplanation:
The sino-atrial (SA) node, in the right atrial wall near the superior vena cava, has the fastest intrinsic firing rate (about 60-100/min), so it sets the heart rhythm.
Not B: the AV node is a backup pacemaker (40-60/min).
Not C: the His bundle fires even more slowly.
Not D: valves are not excitable tissue.
Not E: working ventricular myocardium does not normally show automaticity.

set-03-A-002.originalExplanation:
The QRS complex records depolarisation of the ventricles.
Not A: atrial depolarisation is the P wave.
Not B: atrial repolarisation happens at the same time as the QRS and is hidden by it.
Not D: ventricular repolarisation is the T wave.
Not E: the AV nodal delay is within the PR segment.

set-03-A-003.originalExplanation:
An ECG records the heart's electrical activity, so it can show blocked conduction between atria and ventricles (AV blocks, as PR prolongation, dropped beats or P-QRS dissociation).
Not A: murmurs are mechanical sounds, detected by auscultation or echocardiography.
Not B or C: stroke volume and cardiac output are mechanical/flow measures that need echo, Fick or dilution methods.
Not E: D is correct.

set-03-A-004.originalExplanation:
All three statements describe cardiac output. It is the volume pumped per minute by each ventricle (A). In a steady state that equals the flow through the systemic circulation each minute (B). It is calculated as heart rate x stroke volume (C), e.g. 70 x 70 mL = about 5 L/min.
Not D: it leaves out B, which is also correct.

set-03-A-005.originalExplanation:
Frank-Starling mechanism: more venous return raises end-diastolic volume, which stretches the fibres and produces a stronger contraction, so stroke volume increases.
Not A: the ventricles eject nearly equal volumes, and the mechanism is what keeps them matched.
Not B: intrinsic pacemaker rate is a property of the SA node.
Not C: rate-dependent output is chronotropy.
Not E: timing of contraction is unrelated to the length-tension relationship.

set-03-A-006.originalExplanation:
Protodiastole is the short interval at the start of ventricular relaxation, when ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure. The AV valves are still closed and the semilunar valves are closing (backflow snaps them shut, giving S2).
Not A: AV valves open later, at the end of isovolumetric relaxation.
Not B: both are closed in the next phase, isovolumetric relaxation.
Not C: both are never open together.
Not E: D is correct.

set-03-A-007.originalExplanation:
In exercise, blood flow to working muscles rises many-fold through metabolic vasodilation.
Not A: brain flow stays almost constant because of cerebral autoregulation.
Not B: renal (and splanchnic) flow falls due to sympathetic vasoconstriction, freeing cardiac output for muscle.
Not D or E: these include brain and kidneys, which do not increase.

set-03-A-008.originalExplanation:
In isovolumetric contraction, ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure (AV valves close) but is still below arterial pressure (semilunar valves still closed). Both sets of valves are closed, so volume stays constant while pressure rises.
Not A: both sets are never open together.
Not B: SL valves open only when ejection begins.
Not C: an open AV and closed SL valve describes ventricular filling.
Not E: D is correct.

set-03-A-009.originalExplanation:
The aortic valve closes at the start of ventricular diastole, when aortic pressure exceeds LV pressure. This stops blood flowing back from the aorta into the left ventricle.
Not A: backflow INTO the aorta would come from the ventricle, which the valve does not guard against in diastole.
Not C or D: during ejection the valve is open and flow is forward.
Not E: the aortic valve closes with the SECOND heart sound; S1 is AV valve closure.

set-03-A-010.originalExplanation:
After haemorrhage, falling venous return lowers cardiac output (C). Baroreceptor-driven sympathetic activity constricts veins to mobilise stored blood (A) and constricts skin vessels, causing pallor and coldness (B). So E (a, b and c) is the best answer.
Not D: splenic contraction is an important reservoir response in animals such as dogs and horses but contributes little in humans.

set-03-A-011.originalExplanation:
Heart sounds are mechanical vibrations (mainly from valve closure), heard by auscultation with a stethoscope and recorded graphically by phonocardiography.
Not A: arterial wall pulsations are recorded by sphygmography.
Not B: bioelectrical activity is recorded by the ECG.
Not C: cardiac output needs flow measurement.
Not E: phlebography records the venous pulse.

set-03-A-012.originalExplanation:
The kidney receives about 400 mL/min per 100 g, far more than its metabolic needs, because it must filter plasma.
Not A: the brain gets about 50-55 mL/min/100 g.
Not B: heart muscle gets about 70-80 mL/min/100 g at rest.
Not C: skin gets about 10 mL/min/100 g (very variable with temperature).
Not D: the liver gets about 100 mL/min/100 g.

set-03-A-013.revisionNote: Stem completed by DOMiNANCE. The original gave only the heart rate, so cardiac output could not be calculated.
set-03-A-013.originalExplanation:
Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 70 × 75 mL = 5250 mL/min ≈ 5.25 L/min, a typical resting value.
Not A or B: these would need a stroke volume of only about 49-65 mL.
Not D or E: 8-10 L/min would need a stroke volume of over 110 mL at this rate, as seen in exercise, not rest.

set-03-A-014.originalExplanation:
The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation.
Not A: the PQ (PR) interval is atrial depolarisation plus AV conduction.
Not C: the QT interval covers ventricular depolarisation AND repolarisation (total ventricular electrical systole).
Not D: the ST segment is the plateau, when the ventricles are fully depolarised.
Not E: the T wave is ventricular repolarisation.

set-03-A-015.originalExplanation:
The two ventricles are in series, so their outputs must be equal (100%) over time; otherwise blood would build up in one circulation. The Frank-Starling mechanism corrects small mismatches.
Not A, B, C: lower right-sided output would empty the lungs and congest the systemic veins.
Not E: higher right-sided output would cause pulmonary congestion and oedema.

set-03-A-016.originalExplanation:
During ventricular filling, atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, so the AV valves are open. Arterial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, so the semilunar valves are closed.
Not A: both are never open together.
Not B: this is the ejection phase.
Not D: both closed describes the isovolumetric phases.
Not E: C is correct.

set-03-A-017.originalExplanation:
Sympathetic noradrenaline acting on beta1 receptors increases force (positive inotropy, A), heart metabolism and O2 use (B), and AV conduction velocity (positive dromotropy, C). So E is correct.
Not D: sympathetic stimulation INCREASES excitability (positive bathmotropy).

set-03-A-018.revisionNote: Rewritten by DOMiNANCE as a single-best-answer item. The original combination option ('a and d') was the only way to get both correct features.
set-03-A-018.originalExplanation:
Ventricular action potentials last about 0.25-0.3 s because of a plateau (phase 2), when L-type Ca2+ entry balances K+ efflux. The long plateau gives a long refractory period, so cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised.
Not A: a short action potential (a few ms) is typical of skeletal muscle and nerve.
Not B: ventricular myocytes rest at about -90 mV; slow depolarisation from a less negative potential describes pacemaker cells.
Not C: the ventricular upstroke is carried by fast Na+ channels; Ca2+-driven upstrokes occur in SA and AV nodal cells.
Not E: the refractory period is long, which is exactly what prevents summation.

set-03-A-019.originalExplanation:
Mean arterial pressure is the time-weighted average (integral) of pressure over one cardiac cycle. It is the pressure that drives flow and is about diastolic + one third of pulse pressure.
Not A: pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic.
Not B or C: these are the peak and trough values.
Not E: because diastole is longer, MAP is closer to diastolic than systolic pressure.

set-03-A-020.originalExplanation:
Cycle duration = 60 / heart rate (e.g. 0.8 s at 75 beats/min). Heart rate therefore determines it, and rising rate mostly shortens diastole.
Not A: stroke volume does not set timing.
Not B, C, E: systole, diastole and pause are PARTS of the cycle; they result from heart rate rather than independently determining it.

set-03-A-021.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original had two acceptable answers (ventricular extrasystoles and a prolonged QT).
set-03-A-021.originalExplanation:
Low K+ slows ventricular repolarisation, giving flattened T waves, prominent U waves, ST depression and an apparent long QT (really QU). It also increases ectopic activity and arrhythmias.
Not A: the PR interval may lengthen slightly, not shorten.
Not C: ST DEPRESSION occurs, not elevation.
Not D: tall, peaked T waves are the earliest sign of HYPERkalaemia.
Not E: a short QT suggests hypercalcaemia.

set-03-A-022.revisionNote: Rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original had two correct answers (QRS prolongation and loss of P waves).
set-03-A-022.originalExplanation:
Rising K+ speeds repolarisation, so the first change is tall, narrow, peaked (tented) T waves. As K+ rises further, the PR lengthens, P waves flatten and disappear, the QRS widens, and a sine-wave pattern leads to VF or asystole.
Not B and D: prominent U waves and ST depression with flat T waves are signs of HYPOkalaemia.
Not C: hyperkalaemia SHORTENS the QT; a long QT suggests hypokalaemia or hypocalcaemia.
Not E: the PR interval LENGTHENS in hyperkalaemia.

set-03-A-023.originalExplanation:
Normal LV end-diastolic volume in an adult is about 110-130 mL (often quoted as 120 mL). With a stroke volume of about 70 mL, this gives an ejection fraction of about 55-60%.
Not A to C: these values are closer to end-systolic volume (about 50 mL).
Not D: 70-100 mL is too low for a normal adult LV at end-diastole.

set-03-A-024.originalExplanation:
Purkinje fibres (tertiary pacemakers) have the slowest intrinsic rate, about 20-40 impulses/min. This is why a ventricular escape rhythm is very slow.
Not A or E: His bundle and bundle branches fire at about 40 per minute or slightly lower; in this classic scheme they sit with the junction.
Not B: the AV node fires at 40-60/min.
Not C: the SA node fires at 60-90 (up to 100)/min.

set-03-A-025.originalExplanation:
End-diastolic volume is set mainly by how much blood returns to the heart during diastole, so more venous return gives a higher EDV (preload).
Not A: stroke volume depends on EDV, not the other way round.
Not C: residual volume after the previous contraction (end-systolic volume) does contribute.
Not D: higher aortic pressure raises afterload; EDV may rise only secondarily.
Not E: atrial systole contributes about 20-30% of filling.

set-03-A-026.originalExplanation:
Atrial natriuretic peptide, released when the atria are stretched, is a vasodilator. It also promotes Na+ and water excretion, lowering blood volume and pressure.
Not A: noradrenaline constricts via alpha1 receptors.
Not B: vasopressin (ADH) constricts via V1 receptors.
Not C: serotonin mostly constricts vessels (its effects vary by bed).
Not D: angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor via AT1 receptors.

set-03-A-027.originalExplanation:
The AV node conducts slowest (about 0.02-0.05 m/s) because its cells are small, have few gap junctions and depend on slow Ca2+-driven action potentials. This creates the AV delay.
Not A: atrial muscle conducts at about 0.3-1 m/s.
Not C: the His bundle conducts at about 1-2 m/s.
Not D: Purkinje fibres are the fastest at about 2-4 m/s.
Not E: ventricular muscle conducts at about 0.3-1 m/s.

set-03-A-028.revisionNote: Rewritten by DOMiNANCE. Both noradrenaline and adrenaline act on α and β receptors, so the original had two correct answers. The stem now tests the β2 difference.
set-03-A-028.originalExplanation:
Adrenaline is a potent agonist at all three: α1 (vasoconstriction in skin and gut), β1 (higher heart rate and contractility) and β2 (vasodilation in skeletal muscle, bronchodilation).
Not A: noradrenaline acts on α1 and β1 but is WEAK at β2, so it constricts nearly all vascular beds.
Not C: isoprenaline is a pure β agonist with no α action.
Not D: phenylephrine is a selective α1 agonist.
Not E: dobutamine acts mainly on β1.

set-03-A-029.originalExplanation:
Mitral stenosis obstructs flow from the left atrium into the LV during diastole, giving a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble (often after an opening snap), loudest at the apex (mitral area).
Not A: continuous murmurs suggest e.g. patent ductus arteriosus.
Not B: a systolic murmur at the base suggests aortic or pulmonary stenosis.
Not D: a diastolic murmur at the base suggests aortic or pulmonary regurgitation.
Not E: an apical systolic murmur suggests mitral regurgitation.

set-03-A-030.originalExplanation:
Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) fire more when arterial pO2 falls, and also with high pCO2, high H+ and low perfusion.
Not A: high pressure does not stimulate them (very low pressure can, by reducing their blood supply).
Not C: low pCO2 reduces firing.
Not D: lower H+ (alkalosis) reduces firing.
Not E: hypothermia reduces their activity.

set-03-A-031.revisionNote: Stem clarified by DOMiNANCE ('per 100 g of tissue'). The original did not say whether total or per-gram consumption was meant, which changes the answer.
set-03-A-031.originalExplanation:
At rest the heart uses about 8-10 mL O₂/100 g/min and extracts about 70-75% of the O₂ delivered to it, the highest per-gram consumption of these organs.
Not A: the brain uses about 3.5 mL/100 g/min (large total use because of its size).
Not C: the liver uses about 2-6 mL/100 g/min, depending on the source.
Not D: the kidneys use about 6-7 mL/100 g/min, mostly for Na+ reabsorption, despite their very high blood flow.
Not E: resting skeletal muscle uses only about 0.2 mL/100 g/min (but rises hugely in exercise).

set-03-A-032.originalExplanation:
Right ventricular pressure during systole (about 25 mmHg) is far below aortic pressure, so the RV wall does not squeeze its vessels shut and right coronary flow continues in systole.
Not A: right-dominant circulation is the most common (about 70-85%); left dominance is about 10%.
Not B or D: left coronary flow falls in systole, especially to the subendocardium, which is compressed most.
Not E: right coronary flow is not suspended in systole.

set-03-A-033.originalExplanation:
S2 (closure of aortic and pulmonary valves) is shorter, higher-pitched and usually softer than S1. These semilunar valves are smaller and close sharply against high arterial pressure.
Not A or D: being longer describes S1, which is longer and lower-pitched.
Not B: 'strong' and 'weak' together is self-contradictory.
Not E: S2 is typically softer than S1, especially at the apex.

set-03-A-034.originalExplanation:
Absent P waves with normal QRS and T waves mean the ventricles are activated normally through the His-Purkinje system but the atria are not driving them. This is a junctional (AV nodal) rhythm at about 40-60/min; retrograde P waves may be hidden in the QRS.
Not A: an SA pacemaker produces P waves.
Not C: a His focus is possible but less typical.
Not D or E: Purkinje or ventricular foci produce wide, abnormal QRS complexes.

set-03-A-035.originalExplanation:
Isovolumetric contraction is the first part of ventricular systole (the contraction phase): pressure builds with all valves closed before ejection.
Not A: it comes BEFORE the ejection phase.
Not C: it is systolic, not diastolic.
Not D or E: rapid and slow filling are phases of diastole.

set-03-A-036.originalExplanation:
Arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch are stretch receptors. They respond to the level of pressure and how quickly it changes, and the reflex mainly defends mean arterial pressure.
Not A or B: systolic and diastolic values affect firing, but the regulated variable is mean pressure.
Not C or E: pCO2 and pO2 are sensed by chemoreceptors.

set-03-A-037.originalExplanation:
Asynchronous contraction is the first phase of ventricular systole in the classical phase scheme. Excitation spreads and fibres start contracting at different times, and it ends when the AV valves close and isovolumetric contraction begins.
Not B: it is systolic.
Not C: SL valves close at the start of diastole.
Not D: SL valves open at the end of isovolumetric contraction.
Not E: AV valves open in diastole.

set-03-A-038.originalExplanation:
Einthoven's standard bipolar limb leads are I (right arm to left arm), II (right arm to left leg) and III (left arm to left leg). Each records the potential difference between two limbs.
Not A: aVR, aVL and aVF are augmented UNIPOLAR limb leads.
Not C: V1-V6 are unipolar precordial (chest) leads.
Not D or E: these combinations include unipolar leads.

set-03-A-039.originalExplanation:
In exercise, metabolic vasodilation in the large active muscle mass greatly lowers total peripheral resistance, even though vessels constrict in gut, kidney and inactive tissue.
Not A: stroke volume rises (more venous return and contractility).
Not C: systolic pressure rises.
Not D: heart rate rises.
Not E: muscle blood flow rises many-fold.

set-03-A-040.originalExplanation:
Baroreceptors produce BOTH kinds of reflex. Rising pressure increases their firing, giving a depressor reflex (bradycardia, vasodilation). Falling pressure reduces firing, giving a pressor response (tachycardia, vasoconstriction).
Not B or D: only one direction is wrong.
Not C: baroreceptors reset within days, so they mainly control short-term pressure.
Not E: the Bainbridge reflex comes from atrial volume receptors.

set-03-A-041.originalExplanation:
Sympathetic stimulation acts directly on SA node beta1 receptors, increasing the If and Ca2+ currents and steepening phase 4 depolarisation, which raises heart rate.
Not B: parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation slows the heart.
Not C: low blood pressure raises heart rate only INDIRECTLY, through the baroreceptor reflex.
Not D: it includes B, which is wrong.
Not E: A is correct.

set-03-A-042.originalExplanation:
Long-term blood pressure control is humoral and renal, adjusting blood volume through renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, ADH, natriuretic peptides and pressure natriuresis.
Not A or B: nerve and baroreceptor reflexes act in seconds to minutes and reset within days.
Not D: chemoreceptor reflexes mainly respond to blood gases and are not long-term pressure regulators.
Not E: the hypothalamus modulates cardiovascular control but is not the long-term regulator.

set-03-A-043.originalExplanation:
The SA node is the physiological pacemaker because its intrinsic firing rate is the fastest, and it suppresses slower pacemakers (overdrive suppression).
Not A: the AV node (40-60/min) takes over only if the SA node fails.
Not B: Purkinje fibres (20-40/min) are tertiary pacemakers.
Not C: the AV bundle (His) is also a subsidiary pacemaker.
Not E: D is correct.

set-03-A-044.originalExplanation:
The T wave reflects ventricular repolarisation.
Not A: a resting state gives a flat (isoelectric) baseline, not a wave.
Not B: atrial depolarisation is the P wave.
Not C: SA node activity is too small to appear on the surface ECG.
Not E: Purkinje activation is part of the PR interval and the early QRS.

set-03-A-045.revisionNote: Rewritten by DOMiNANCE as a calculation. Quoted normal EDV varies between textbooks (about 120-140 mL), so the original was not reliably scoreable.
set-03-A-045.originalExplanation:
Ejection fraction = stroke volume / end-diastolic volume, so EDV = SV / EF = 70 / 0.55 ≈ 127 mL, i.e. about 130 mL (normal range about 110-140 mL).
Not A: 50 mL is about the END-SYSTOLIC volume (EDV - SV).
Not B: 70 mL is the stroke volume itself.
Not C: 100 mL would give an EF of 70%.
Not E: 200 mL would give an EF of 35%, as in a dilated, failing ventricle.

set-03-A-046.originalExplanation:
Vagal acetylcholine acts on M2 receptors in the SA node, opening K+ channels and reducing the If current. This slows the firing rate (bradycardia).
Not A: vagal activity tends to LOWER blood pressure.
Not B: tachycardia results from vagal withdrawal or sympathetic activity.
Not D: cardiac output falls with a slower rate.
Not E: the vagus has little effect on ventricular force, so stroke volume does not significantly rise.

set-03-A-047.originalExplanation:
The dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure curve marks aortic valve closure. As the ventricle relaxes, blood briefly flows back against the valve; when it shuts, the elastic rebound gives the notch.
Not A or B: AV valve closure happens at the start of systole (S1).
Not D: pulmonary valve closure appears on the pulmonary artery trace, not the aortic one.
Not E: AV valve opening marks the start of filling.

set-03-A-048.originalExplanation:
By Poiseuille's law, resistance is proportional to 1/r^4. Small changes in vessel radius (mainly arterioles) therefore change resistance far more than any other factor, which is why arteriolar tone controls regional flow.
Not A: viscosity matters but changes little in health.
Not B: vessel length is essentially fixed.
Not C: laminar flow is a flow pattern, not a determinant of resistance.
Not E: venous valves direct flow but contribute little resistance.

set-03-A-049.originalExplanation:
Working myocardium is a functional syncytium: cells are separate but electrically coupled by gap junctions, so excitation spreads through the whole chamber and it contracts as one unit.
Not B: the cells keep their own membranes; only ions and small molecules pass through gap junctions, with no continuous cytoplasm.
Not C: pacemaking belongs to specialised conducting tissue.
Not D: the junctions ALLOW ion flow.
Not E: the heart obeys the all-or-none law, so a threshold stimulus excites all fibres.

set-03-A-050.originalExplanation:
In this course a normal adult resting heart rate is about 60-90 beats/min (60-100 in many texts).
Not A: 100-140 is tachycardia.
Not B: 40-60 is bradycardia and the AV junctional rate.
Not C: about 50 is bradycardic (normal only in trained athletes).
Not E: 20-40 is a ventricular (Purkinje) escape rate.

set-03-A-051.originalExplanation:
A ventricular extrasystole usually does not conduct back to reset the SA node. The next sinus impulse falls in the ventricles' refractory period and is blocked, and the following one comes on time. So the gap around the premature beat equals two normal cycles: a full compensatory pause.
Not A or B: atrial extrasystoles reset the SA node, giving an incomplete pause.
Not D or E: in atrial fibrillation or flutter there is no regular sinus rhythm to compensate for.

set-03-A-052.originalExplanation:
Cycle duration = 60 / heart rate (e.g. 0.8 s at 75 beats/min). Heart rate therefore determines it, and rising rate mostly shortens diastole.
Not A: stroke volume does not set timing.
Not B, C, E: systole, diastole and pause are PARTS of the cycle; they result from heart rate rather than independently determining it.

set-03-A-053.originalExplanation:
The sinus (SA) node sets the normal heart rhythm because its spontaneous depolarisation is fastest.
Not A, B, D, E: the His bundle, AV node, Purkinje fibres and bundle branches are slower subsidiary pacemakers and take over only if the SA node fails or conduction is blocked.

set-03-A-054.originalExplanation:
Tachycardia is a heart rate above the normal resting range (above about 90-100 beats/min).
Not A: tachypnoea means rapid BREATHING.
Not B: bradycardia is a SLOW heart rate.
Not C: atrial fibrillation is chaotic atrial activity with an irregular ventricular rate.
Not D: atrial flutter is a specific rapid atrial rhythm. Neither C nor D simply means 'increased heart rate'.

set-03-A-055.originalExplanation:
When the AV node (junction) acts as pacemaker, its intrinsic rate is about 40-60 beats/min.
Not A or C: 60-90 and about 75 are sinus rates.
Not B: 20-40 is a ventricular (Purkinje) escape rate.
Not E: '8-120' is not a physiological pacemaker range.

set-03-A-056.originalExplanation:
Automaticity (spontaneous generation of impulses) occurs in cardiac conducting system cells, some neurons (e.g. respiratory rhythm generators) and some smooth muscle cells (e.g. gut pacemaker activity, ureter).
Not A: cardiac muscle is not the only automatic tissue, and working myocytes are not automatic.
Not B: skeletal muscle needs nerve stimulation.
Not D: most excitable tissues are not automatic.
Not E: smooth muscle is not the only type.

set-03-A-057.originalExplanation:
Ventricular myocyte action potentials have rapid depolarisation (phase 0: fast Na+ influx) followed by slow repolarisation (a long plateau from L-type Ca2+ influx balanced by K+ efflux, then phase 3).
Not A: this suits pacemaker cells only in part, with their slow upstroke.
Not C: rapid depolarisation and repolarisation describes nerve and skeletal muscle.
Not D: depolarisation is fast.
Not E: slow waves with spikes describe gut smooth muscle.

set-03-A-058.originalExplanation:
The P wave reflects atrial depolarisation.
Not A: atrial repolarisation is hidden within the QRS.
Not B: ventricular depolarisation is the QRS.
Not D: hyperpolarisation is not a normal ECG wave.
Not E: the time from SA node to ventricles is the PR interval, not the P wave.

set-03-A-059.originalExplanation:
Asynchronous contraction is the first phase of ventricular systole in the classical phase scheme. Excitation spreads and fibres start contracting at different times, and it ends when the AV valves close and isovolumetric contraction begins.
Not B: it is systolic.
Not C: SL valves close at the start of diastole.
Not D: SL valves open at the end of isovolumetric contraction.
Not E: AV valves open in diastole.

set-03-A-060.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original combination option ('a, b and c') contained statements that are not always true.
set-03-A-060.originalExplanation:
In complete heart block no atrial impulses reach the ventricles. The atria follow the SA node while the ventricles follow an escape pacemaker (junctional about 40-60/min with narrow QRS, or ventricular about 20-40/min with wide QRS), so P waves and QRS complexes 'march through' each other (AV dissociation).
Not A: this is first-degree block.
Not B: this is Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree block.
Not C: this is Mobitz II second-degree block.
Not D: this is atrial fibrillation.

set-03-A-061.originalExplanation:
Resting stroke volume is about 70 mL (roughly 60-80 mL): end-diastolic volume (about 120 mL) minus end-systolic volume (about 50 mL).
Not A: beats/min is a unit of heart rate.
Not C: 5.2 L is cardiac output per minute.
Not D: 0.5 L per beat is far too large.
Not E: mmHg is a unit of pressure.

set-03-A-062.revisionNote: Stem and options rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original option C ('the direction of the electrical forces of the ventricular muscle') described what the axis IS, which made it competitive with the keyed answer.
set-03-A-062.originalExplanation:
The cardiac (QRS) axis is the mean direction of ventricular depolarisation in the frontal plane. It is worked out from the net (positive minus negative) QRS deflections in the limb leads: Einthoven's standard leads I, II and III, usually checked against aVF and the other augmented leads on the hexaxial reference system.
Not A or E: chest leads record the HORIZONTAL plane, so they cannot give the frontal-plane axis.
Not C: P waves give the atrial (P-wave) axis, not the cardiac electrical axis.
Not D: T waves give the axis of ventricular repolarisation (the T axis), which is a different vector.

set-03-A-063.originalExplanation:
The augmented unipolar limb leads are aVR, aVL and aVF. Each compares one limb with the average of the other two, and they are 'augmented' to increase voltage.
Not A: I, II, III are bipolar standard leads.
Not C: it includes the bipolar leads.
Not D: V1-V6 are unipolar chest leads, not augmented limb leads.
Not E: it includes chest leads.

set-03-A-064.originalExplanation:
The mitral area is at the apex: the 5th left intercostal space, just medial to the midclavicular line.
Not A: 2nd right intercostal space is the aortic area.
Not C: the tricuspid area is at the lower left sternal border (4th-5th space); the 'right of the sternum' location in this option is not the mitral area.
Not D: 2nd left intercostal space is the pulmonary area.
Not E: 3rd left intercostal space is Erb's point.

set-03-A-065.originalExplanation:
The plateau (phase 2) is caused by slow Ca2+ influx through L-type channels, balanced against K+ efflux. This keeps the membrane depolarised for about 200 ms and triggers Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release for contraction.
Not A: K+ efflux alone would repolarise the cell (phase 3).
Not B: fast Na+ influx causes the phase 0 upstroke and inactivates quickly.
Not C: K+ normally flows OUT, not in.
Not E: Na+ influx with K+ outflow does not explain the plateau.

set-03-A-066.originalExplanation:
Extrasystoles are premature beats arising from an ectopic focus, a disturbance of excitability (C). They interrupt the basic rhythm only now and then (D). So E (c and d) is correct.
Not A: rates of 230-250/min describe paroxysmal tachycardia or flutter.
Not B: disturbances of conductivity are heart blocks.

set-03-A-067.originalExplanation:
In the classical classification of the electrical axis (alpha angle), the 'indifferent' (intermediate, normal) position is about +30 to +60 degrees.
Not A: +60 to +90 is the vertical position.
Not D: +30 to -30 includes the horizontal position and the start of left deviation.
Not E: beyond -30 is left axis deviation.
Not C: 'from -90 upward' is not a defined normal type.

set-03-A-068.originalExplanation:
Kinins (bradykinin, kallidin) are potent vasodilators that act through endothelial NO and prostacyclin release, and they increase capillary permeability.
Not A: norepinephrine constricts via alpha1.
Not B: epinephrine constricts most beds via alpha1, though it dilates skeletal-muscle vessels via beta2.
Not C: serotonin mainly constricts.
Not D: angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor.

set-03-A-069.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original had two acceptable answers (the range 60-90 mmHg and the single value 75 mmHg).
set-03-A-069.originalExplanation:
Normal resting diastolic pressure is about 60-90 mmHg (typically about 80 mmHg).
Not A: below about 60 mmHg is low and may threaten coronary perfusion, which mostly occurs in diastole.
Not C: a diastolic pressure of 95-110 mmHg indicates hypertension.
Not D and E: these are systolic-range values; as diastolic pressures they would mean severe hypertension.

set-03-A-070.originalExplanation:
The pressure gradient in the circulation is set by cardiac output and total peripheral resistance (P = Q x R), and resistance depends on blood viscosity. Blood volume affects filling and therefore output and pressure. Minute respiratory volume (ventilation) is a respiratory variable and has no direct effect, so B is correct.
Not A, C, D, E: each directly affects pressure.

set-03-A-071.originalExplanation:
In isovolumetric relaxation, ventricular pressure has fallen below arterial pressure (SL valves closed) but is still above atrial pressure (AV valves closed). With all valves closed, pressure falls but volume stays constant.
Not A: both are never open together.
Not B: SL valves are open during ejection.
Not C: this describes ventricular filling.
Not E: D is correct.

set-03-A-072.originalExplanation:
S1 marks the start of ventricular systole. It is caused mainly by closure of the AV (mitral and tricuspid) valves as the contracting ventricles raise pressure above atrial pressure, together with vibration of the tensed ventricular walls and blood. So A and B together (E) is correct.
Not C: SL valve closure produces S2.
Not D: S1 is systolic, not diastolic.

set-03-A-073.originalExplanation:
Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate (B, C), and stroke volume depends on preload, afterload and contractility (D). So E is correct.
Not A: vital capacity is a lung volume and has no direct link to cardiac output.

set-03-A-074.originalExplanation:
Intracardiac (intrinsic) regulation is the heart's self-adjustment without nerves or hormones. It adapts to venous return through the heterometric Frank-Starling mechanism and to changes in peripheral resistance through homeometric mechanisms such as the Anrep effect.
Not A, B, C: reflex, neural and humoral regulation are EXTRACARDIAC.
Not E: automaticity generates the rhythm but does not adapt output to load.

set-03-A-075.originalExplanation:
High extracellular K+ (above about 8 mmol/L) depolarises the resting membrane and inactivates fast Na+ channels. Excitability and conduction fail and the heart stops in a relaxed (diastolic) state; this is the principle of cardioplegia solutions.
Not A: high Ca2+ tends to cause arrest in contraction (systole).
Not B, C, E: catecholamines, glucocorticoids and thyroid hormones increase rate and/or contractility.

set-03-A-076.originalExplanation:
Cycle duration = 60 / heart rate = 60 / 60 = 1 s.
Not A: 0.5 s corresponds to 120 beats/min.
Not B: 0.8 s corresponds to 75 beats/min.
Not D: 0.2 s would mean 300 beats/min.
Not E: C is correct.

set-03-A-077.originalExplanation:
Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic pressure (e.g. 120 - 80 = 40 mmHg). It reflects mainly stroke volume and arterial compliance.
Not A or C: it is a difference, not a value near either pressure.
Not B: the simple average of systolic and diastolic is not a standard measure; MAP is about diastolic + one third of pulse pressure.
Not E: one third of pulse pressure (not of MAP) is added to diastolic pressure to estimate MAP.

set-03-A-078.originalExplanation:
The cardiovascular (vasomotor and cardioinhibitory) centre is in the medulla oblongata, including the nucleus tractus solitarius, rostral ventrolateral medulla and nucleus ambiguus/dorsal vagal nucleus.
Not A or C: the hypothalamus and cortex influence it but are higher centres.
Not B: the midbrain is not the main centre.
Not E: T1-L2 spinal segments contain the sympathetic preganglionic neurons it controls.

set-03-A-079.originalExplanation:
In the pulmonary circulation, deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries to the lungs.
Not A: the aorta receives blood from the LEFT ventricle.
Not C: the right atrium empties into the RIGHT ventricle.
Not D: the right atrium does not connect directly to the lungs.
Not E: the left ventricle supplies the systemic circulation.

set-03-A-080.originalExplanation:
In the systemic circulation, oxygenated blood leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve into the aorta.
Not B: the right ventricle supplies the pulmonary trunk.
Not C: that is the pulmonary circulation.
Not D: lungs to left atrium is the END of the pulmonary circulation.
Not E: the right atrium does not send blood directly to the lungs.

set-03-A-081.originalExplanation: Heart rate is the NUMBER of cycles per minute, a rate rather than an event within a single cycle, so C is the exception. A single cardiac cycle includes the spread of excitation from the SA node (A), valve opening and closing (B), and pressure (D) and volume (E) changes in every chamber.

set-03-A-082.revisionNote: Rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original asked which substance does NOT regulate blood pressure and keyed 'nitric acid', which was almost certainly a typo for nitric oxide, and nitric oxide is a key regulator. The item now asks where each substance comes from.
set-03-A-082.originalExplanation:
Nitric oxide is made by endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) in response to shear stress, acetylcholine and bradykinin. It diffuses into vascular smooth muscle, raises cGMP and causes vasodilation, giving continuous tonic control of vascular resistance and blood pressure.
Not A: ADH (vasopressin) is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
Not B: ANP is secreted by atrial myocytes when the atria are stretched.
Not C: renin is released by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney.
Not E: epinephrine comes from the adrenal medulla.
All five help regulate blood pressure, so the question tests their SOURCE.

set-03-A-083.originalExplanation:
Capillaries are the exchange vessels. They have walls one endothelial cell thick, an enormous total surface area and slow flow, which allows diffusion of gases, nutrients and wastes.
Not A: arterioles are resistance vessels.
Not B: arteries are conducting and pressure-reservoir vessels.
Not C: veins are capacitance (blood-reservoir) vessels.
Not E: venules allow some exchange and leukocyte migration but are not the main exchange site.

set-03-A-084.originalExplanation:
The Frank-Starling law: within physiological limits, force of contraction increases with the initial (end-diastolic) length of the muscle fibres. More stretch improves actin-myosin overlap and troponin's Ca2+ sensitivity.
Not A: pacemaker activity sets rate.
Not B: the AV nodal delay is a timing feature.
Not D: respiratory rate is unrelated.
Not E: the ST segment is an ECG feature, not a cause of force.

set-03-A-085.originalExplanation:
The inferior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the lower body to the right atrium, as does the superior vena cava from the upper body.
Not A: the left atrium receives the pulmonary veins.
Not C: the aorta carries blood away from the left ventricle.
Not D or E: the veins drain into the atria, not directly into the ventricles.

set-03-A-086.originalExplanation:
The SA node is the normal pacemaker because it has the fastest spontaneous depolarisation rate (about 60-100/min).
Not A: Purkinje fibres are the slowest (20-40/min).
Not B or C: bundle branches and His bundle are subsidiary pacemakers.
Not D: the AV node is the secondary pacemaker (40-60/min).

set-03-A-087.originalExplanation:
The tricuspid valve, with three cusps, lies between the right atrium and right ventricle.
Not A or B: the septa, not valves, separate the two atria and the two ventricles.
Not D: the mitral (bicuspid) valve is between the left atrium and ventricle.
Not E: the right ventricle opens into the pulmonary trunk through the pulmonary valve; the aorta is guarded by the aortic valve on the left.

set-03-A-088.originalExplanation:
During ventricular systole, LV pressure exceeds left atrial pressure; the closed mitral valve stops blood flowing back from the LV into the LA. Regurgitation through this valve produces an apical systolic murmur.
Not A: in diastole, flow from LA to LV is forward.
Not C: this concerns the tricuspid valve.
Not D: flow from LV to aorta is normal ejection, not backflow.
Not E: this concerns the pulmonary valve.

set-03-A-089.originalExplanation:
The AV node conducts slowest (about 0.02-0.05 m/s), giving the AV delay that lets the atria finish filling the ventricles.
Not A: the SA node also conducts slowly, but the AV node is the classic slowest point.
Not B: atrial muscle conducts at about 0.3-1 m/s.
Not C: Purkinje fibres are the fastest (about 2-4 m/s).
Not E: the His bundle conducts at about 1-2 m/s.

set-03-A-090.originalExplanation:
The intercalated discs between myocytes contain gap junctions (connexin channels) that let ions flow directly from cell to cell, so excitation spreads as if through one cell. This makes the heart a functional syncytium.
Not A: striations reflect sarcomere organisation.
Not B: branching helps form a network but does not couple cells electrically.
Not D: desmosomes provide MECHANICAL attachment.
Not E: Ca2+ affects contraction strength, not electrical coupling.

set-03-A-091.originalExplanation:
Bathmotropy means excitability. Sympathetic stimulation (noradrenaline at beta1 receptors) increases excitability, a positive bathmotropic effect, along with positive chrono-, ino- and dromotropic effects.
Not A: vagal stimulation is negatively bathmotropic.
Not C or D: atropine and vagotomy only REMOVE vagal inhibition rather than directly stimulating the heart.
Not E: raised K+ depolarises cells and inactivates Na+ channels, reducing excitability.

set-03-A-092.originalExplanation:
Myocardial hypoxia releases vasodilator metabolites (adenosine, K+, H+, CO2, NO), which dilate coronary arterioles and increase flow; metabolic control dominates coronary regulation.
Not A: early systole compresses intramural LV vessels, so flow is LOWEST then.
Not C: hypothermia lowers metabolic demand and flow.
Not D: vagal stimulation slows the heart, lowering demand, so flow does not rise significantly.
Not E: AV block slows the ventricular rate and reduces demand.

set-03-A-093.originalExplanation:
Coronary blood flow is set mainly by local metabolic activity: myocardial O2 demand produces adenosine and other vasodilators, because the heart already extracts most of the O2 delivered and can only meet demand by raising flow.
Not B: skin flow is controlled mainly by sympathetic nerves for thermoregulation.
Not C: gland flow is largely neurally linked to secretion.
Not D: lung flow is passive and shaped by hypoxic vasoconstriction.
Not E: renal flow is autoregulated (myogenic, tubuloglomerular feedback) to stabilise filtration, not matched to metabolism.

set-03-A-094.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original omitted the endothelial cells that actually form the barrier, so no option was fully correct.
set-03-A-094.originalExplanation:
The barrier itself is the brain capillary endothelium: continuous, non-fenestrated cells joined by tight junctions (claudins, occludin), with few transport vesicles. Astrocyte end-feet and pericytes induce and support it.
Not A: oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons, not capillaries.
Not B: microglia are the brain's resident immune cells.
Not D: ependymal cells line the ventricles; the choroid plexus epithelium forms the blood-CSF barrier, a separate barrier.
