Not E: brain capillaries have NO fenestrations; fenestrated capillaries occur in the circumventricular organs, which lie outside the barrier.

set-03-A-095.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original had two correct answers ('higher in frequency' and 'occasionally split').
set-03-A-095.originalExplanation:
S2 is caused by closure of the aortic and pulmonary (semilunar) valves at the start of diastole. These smaller valves snap shut against high arterial pressure, so S2 is shorter (about 0.11 s vs 0.15 s) and higher-pitched ('dup' vs 'lub'). It is normally split in inspiration.
Not A: longer and lower-pitched describes S1.
Not C: AV valve closure produces S1.
Not D: S1 marks the onset of systole; S2 marks its end.
Not E: S2 is loudest at the BASE (aortic and pulmonary areas); S1 is loudest at the apex.

set-03-A-096.originalExplanation:
During exercise, the higher cardiac output recruits previously closed pulmonary capillaries and distends open ones, so pulmonary vascular resistance FALLS and pulmonary pressure rises only slightly.
Not A: PVR is about one-tenth of systemic resistance.
Not B: low alveolar O2 causes hypoxic vasoconstriction, which INCREASES resistance.
Not C: resistance is pressure difference divided by flow (e.g. mmHg per L/min).
Not E: sympathetic control of pulmonary vessels is weak, and the circulation is mostly passively regulated.

set-03-A-097.revisionNote: Rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original said cerebral vessels are 'not under sympathetic control', which is too absolute, and 'cardiac' was also a defensible answer.
set-03-A-097.originalExplanation:
Cerebral vessels have sympathetic innervation, but their flow is dominated by local control: PaCO₂, metabolic factors and myogenic autoregulation keep flow almost constant at about 50-55 mL/100 g/min. Sympathetic stimulation has only a small effect.
Not B, C, D: splanchnic, renal and cutaneous beds are strongly constricted by sympathetic nerves (e.g. in haemorrhage, exercise and cold), which redistributes cardiac output.
Not E: resting skeletal-muscle vessels have high sympathetic tone, though metabolites override it during exercise.

set-03-A-098.originalExplanation:
As the ventricles contract, the base (AV valve plane) is pulled down towards the fairly fixed apex, shortening the ventricle along its long axis.
Not A: the threefold wall difference applies to the VENTRICLES (LV vs RV); the atrial walls are similar.
Not B: excitation starts at the SA node in the RIGHT atrium.
Not C: the fibrous skeleton blocks direct atrial-ventricular muscle conduction, so the only route is through the AV node and His bundle.
Not D: atrial systole comes before ventricular systole.

set-03-A-099.originalExplanation:
As the cuff deflates, the first tapping Korotkoff sounds (phase I) mark the systolic pressure: blood begins to spurt through the partly compressed artery.
Not A: the sounds come from turbulence in the brachial artery, not the heart.
Not C: diastolic pressure is taken at disappearance (phase V) or muffling (phase IV), not at the loudest sounds.
Not D: palpatory readings tend to be LOWER, so auscultatory systolic is higher.
Not E: LARGER arms need wider cuffs; a cuff too small overestimates pressure.

set-03-A-100.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original keyed answer ('the period of ventricular depolarisation') was only approximately correct.
set-03-A-100.originalExplanation:
While fast Na+ channels are inactivated, from phase 0 through the plateau to about -50 mV in phase 3 (about 200-250 ms), no stimulus however strong can trigger another action potential.
Not A: ventricular refractory periods are LONGER than atrial ones (about 0.25 s vs 0.15 s).
Not B: it coincides with most of CONTRACTION; by relaxation the muscle is in its relative refractory period.
Not D: this describes the RELATIVE refractory period.
Not E: vagal stimulation shortens ATRIAL refractoriness and has little effect on the ventricles.

set-03-A-101.originalExplanation:
Pressing on the eyeballs triggers the oculocardiac (Aschner-Dagnini) reflex. The ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve carries the signal to the vagal nuclei, causing bradycardia.
Not A: the Goltz reflex is bradycardia or arrest from a blow or tapping on the abdomen.
Not B: a pressor reflex raises pressure.
Not C: the Bezold-Jarisch reflex comes from ventricular receptors (bradycardia, hypotension).
Not E: 'depressor reflex' is a general term; the specific named reflex is D.

set-03-A-102.originalExplanation:
Cycle duration = 60 / heart rate = 60 / 75 = 0.8 s (about 0.3 s systole and 0.5 s diastole).
Not A: 1 s corresponds to 60 beats/min.
Not B: 0.6 s corresponds to 100 beats/min.
Not C: 1.2 s corresponds to 50 beats/min.
Not E: 1.5 s corresponds to 40 beats/min.

set-03-A-103.originalExplanation:
During exercise, sympathetic vasoconstriction diverts blood from splanchnic, renal and inactive tissues, which helps send cardiac output to the dilated active muscles.
Not A: sympathetic outflow to exercising muscle actually rises, but local metabolites override it (functional sympatholysis).
Not B: capillaries have no smooth muscle; arterioles and precapillary sphincters relax.
Not C: arterial pressure rises.
Not E: the muscle pump and venous valves keep venous pressure in exercising limbs low.

set-03-A-104.originalExplanation:
SA node cells have an unstable resting potential: in phase 4 they slowly depolarise (funny current If, then T-type and L-type Ca2+ currents) until they reach threshold. This lets them generate impulses on their own.
Not A: the SA node is only in the RIGHT atrium.
Not B: it is innervated by AUTONOMIC (vagal and sympathetic) nerves, not somatic nerves.
Not C: a denervated SA node still fires (e.g. transplanted hearts).
Not D: SA-to-AV conduction is through atrial muscle and internodal pathways, not Purkinje bundles.

set-03-A-105.originalExplanation:
S1 happens at the start of ventricular systole, when rising ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure and the AV valves close.
Not A: semilunar valve closure is S2.
Not B: the P wave (atrial depolarisation) comes BEFORE S1.
Not C: atrial pressure rises slightly (c wave) as the closed AV valves bulge back.
Not E: the A wave is atrial contraction, which comes before S1.

set-03-A-106.revisionNote: Rewritten by DOMiNANCE to test why the refractory period matters. The original keyed answer ('lasts till cardiac contraction') was only approximately correct.
set-03-A-106.originalExplanation:
The refractory period (about 250 ms) lasts nearly as long as the contraction itself, so the heart cannot be re-excited until it has started to relax. Contractions therefore cannot summate into tetanus, and the heart must relax and refill between beats.
Not A: atrial and ventricular sequencing comes from the AV nodal delay.
Not B: refractoriness does not set filling time; heart rate does.
Not C: summation is exactly what the long refractory period prevents (unlike skeletal muscle).
Not E: it PROTECTS against premature re-excitation.

set-03-A-107.originalExplanation:
Higher end-diastolic filling pressure means greater end-diastolic volume and fibre stretch, so contraction is stronger (Frank-Starling).
Not B: high K+ depolarises cells and weakens contraction, and can cause diastolic arrest.
Not C: low Ca2+ reduces contractile force.
Not D: low Mg2+ mainly causes arrhythmias.
Not E: lower afterload lets the ventricle shorten more and eject more, but it does not increase the force developed by the muscle.

set-03-A-108.originalExplanation:
Parasympathetic (vagal) activation releases acetylcholine on M2 receptors in the SA node, slowing the heart (bradycardia) and AV conduction.
Not A: it tends to lower, not raise, blood pressure.
Not B: tachycardia results from sympathetic activity or vagal withdrawal.
Not D: vagal supply to the ventricles is sparse, so stroke volume does not rise.
Not E: C is correct.

set-03-A-109.originalExplanation:
Cardiac output is defined as the volume pumped by EACH ventricle per minute, expressed in L/min (about 5 L/min at rest).
Not B: 2.0 L/min is far too low for a resting adult.
Not C: 10 L/min occurs only with moderate exertion.
Not D: cold causes skin vasoconstriction and has no major effect on output (shivering may raise it slightly).
Not E: a denervated heart still raises output in exercise, through circulating catecholamines and the Frank-Starling mechanism.

set-03-A-110.originalExplanation:
Raising the arm above heart level adds a negative hydrostatic column (about 0.77 mmHg per cm above the heart), so brachial pressure falls.
Not A: the pulse wave travels at about 4-10 m/s, far faster than blood itself (about 0.2-0.5 m/s).
Not B: stiffer walls INCREASE pulse pressure.
Not C: distal occlusion raises pressure only slightly, not markedly.
Not E: peripheral wave reflection usually makes brachial pulse pressure LARGER than aortic.

set-03-A-111.originalExplanation:
Arterioles are the main resistance vessels. Their smooth-muscle tone creates the largest pressure drop in the circulation, sets total peripheral resistance (the afterload against which the ventricles eject) and controls flow into capillary beds.
Not A: exchange is a capillary function.
Not B: veins hold most of the blood.
Not C: smoothing of pressure fluctuations is mainly done by the elastic arteries (Windkessel effect).
Not E: veins are the blood reservoirs.

set-03-A-112.originalExplanation:
Without nerves, the heart still adjusts stroke volume intrinsically. Greater end-diastolic fibre length gives a stronger contraction (Frank-Starling), so stroke volume rises.
Not B: lower resistance can raise stroke volume briefly, but stroke volume cannot stay above venous return; A is the main intrinsic mechanism.
Not C: falling blood volume reduces filling and stroke volume.
Not D: lower RV output reduces LV filling.
Not E: venodilation pools blood and reduces venous return.

set-03-A-113.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE. The original had three correct answers (A, C and D).
set-03-A-113.originalExplanation:
Peripheral arteries are stiffer and reflected pressure waves add to the forward wave, so systolic pressure and pulse pressure are amplified towards the periphery. Mean pressure falls only slightly.
Not A: peripheral arteries become relatively MORE muscular and less elastic.
Not B: smaller diameters and lower velocities make turbulence LESS likely.
Not D: mean pressure FALLS slightly, because of frictional losses, which is what drives flow.
Not E: arterial pO₂ stays essentially unchanged until blood reaches the capillaries.

set-03-A-114.originalExplanation:
Vagal stimulation releases acetylcholine at the SA node, slowing its firing and so decreasing heart rate.
Not A: atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and INCREASES heart rate.
Not C: glucocorticoids enhance catecholamine effects and do not slow the heart.
Not D: Ca2+ mainly increases contractility.
Not E: adrenaline increases heart rate through beta1 receptors.

set-03-A-115.originalExplanation:
Excess aldosterone (e.g. primary hyperaldosteronism, Conn's syndrome) causes renal Na+ and water retention and expands blood volume, producing systemic hypertension (often with hypokalaemia).
Not A: chronic hypoxia causes PULMONARY hypertension through hypoxic vasoconstriction.
Not C: excess insulin is not a classic direct cause.
Not D: LV hypertrophy is a CONSEQUENCE of hypertension, not a cause.
Not E: ventricular fibrillation produces no effective output and pressure collapses.

set-03-A-116.originalExplanation:
Diastolic pressure depends mainly on how quickly blood runs off from the arteries during diastole, which is set by peripheral (arteriolar) resistance; heart rate also contributes by changing the length of diastole.
Not A: blood volume influences all pressures through cardiac output but is not the main determinant of diastolic pressure.
Not B: viscosity changes little normally.
Not C: cardiac performance (stroke volume) mainly affects SYSTOLIC and pulse pressure.
Not E: vessel length is essentially constant.

set-03-A-117.originalExplanation:
In AF the atria fire chaotically at about 350-600/min, but the AV node's refractoriness lets only some impulses through. The ventricular rate is therefore much lower and irregularly irregular.
Not A: the ECG shows fibrillatory (f) waves, not true P waves, so there is still evidence of atrial activity.
Not C: respiratory sinus arrhythmia needs sinus rhythm.
Not D: the ventricular rate cannot exceed the atrial rate.
Not E: QRS complexes are usually narrow and normal unless there is bundle branch block.

set-03-A-118.originalExplanation:
Fenestrated capillaries have pores (fenestrae, about 60-80 nm) in their endothelial cells, allowing rapid exchange. They are found in renal glomeruli, endocrine glands, the intestinal mucosa and choroid plexus.
Not B: most tissues (muscle, skin, lung) have continuous capillaries.
Not C: exchange goes in both directions.
Not D: capillaries have no smooth muscle.
Not E: the kidney has fenestrated capillaries, but the liver has discontinuous sinusoids, so E is only partly true.

set-03-A-119.originalExplanation:
MAP is about diastolic + one third of pulse pressure (e.g. 80 + 40/3 = about 93 mmHg). This is because the heart spends about two thirds of each cycle in diastole at rest.
Not A: MAP is closer to DIASTOLIC pressure.
Not B: the simple average overestimates MAP at normal heart rates.
Not D: systolic minus diastolic is pulse pressure.
Not E: the formula is wrong (it would exceed systolic).

set-03-A-120.revisionNote: Options rewritten by DOMiNANCE so that only one is correct. The original had three correct answers (A, B and C), and its review note contained stray reference links.
set-03-A-120.originalExplanation:
Cardiac output is the volume pumped by EACH ventricle per minute (CO = stroke volume × heart rate, about 70 mL × 70/min ≈ 5 L/min at rest). The two ventricles are in series, so in a steady state RV output = LV output = systemic flow.
Not A: volume per beat is the stroke volume.
Not B: adding both ventricles double-counts the same blood (it would give about 10 L/min), a common misconception.
Not D: this is the end-diastolic volume (about 120 mL), which sets preload.
Not E: this is the end-systolic volume (about 50 mL); EDV - ESV = stroke volume.

set-03-A-121.originalExplanation:
Pulse wave velocity depends on the properties of the arterial wall: stiffness (elastic modulus), wall thickness and lumen radius (Moens-Korteweg equation). Stiffer walls transmit the wave faster.
Not A: the wave travels far faster than blood and is independent of blood velocity.
Not B: velocity is higher in smaller, stiffer peripheral arteries.
Not D: arteries stiffen with age, so pulse wave velocity increases.
Not E: it is HIGHER, not lower, in smaller arteries.

set-03-A-122.originalExplanation:
Stiff arterial walls reduce compliance, so the same stroke volume produces a higher systolic peak. Diastolic pressure tends to fall because there is less elastic recoil, and pulse pressure widens (isolated systolic hypertension of the elderly).
Not A: compliance DECREASES.
Not C: diastolic pressure tends to fall or stay the same.
Not D: peripheral resistance is set by arterioles, not large-artery stiffness.
Not E: breathing frequency is unrelated.

set-03-A-123.originalExplanation:
In LV failure the ventricle cannot empty properly, so pressure backs up into the left atrium and pulmonary veins. This raises pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, causing congestion and pulmonary oedema.
Not A: right atrial pressure rises only later, if right heart failure follows.
Not B: ejection fraction usually FALLS.
Not D: lung compliance falls as the lungs become congested.
Not E: oedema and breathlessness worsen when LYING down (orthopnoea) and improve when sitting or standing.

set-03-A-124.originalExplanation: Effective filtration pressure is set by the Starling forces: capillary hydrostatic (haemodynamic) pressure (A), plasma colloid osmotic pressure (B), tissue fluid hydrostatic pressure (D) and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure (E). Intrapleural pressure (C) acts within the thorax for lung mechanics and is not a Starling force in systemic capillaries.

set-03-A-125.originalExplanation:
At rest, vagal tone holds the heart well below the SA node's intrinsic rate (about 100/min). Blocking the vagus (e.g. atropine or vagotomy) removes this brake and heart rate increases.
Not A: rate rises, not falls.
Not B or C: stroke volume may fall slightly with shorter filling time, but cardiac output usually stays the same or rises.
Not E: activity changes because vagal tone is normally present.

set-03-A-126.originalExplanation:
The plateau (phase 2) of contractile myocyte action potentials comes from Ca2+ influx through L-type (slow) Ca2+ channels, balanced by K+ efflux. This Ca2+ also triggers SR Ca2+ release for contraction.
Not A or D: Na+ entry causes the rapid upstroke (phase 0), and the fast Na+ channels then inactivate.
Not C: a large rise in K+ permeability causes repolarisation (phase 3).
Not E: a DECREASE in Ca2+ entry would shorten the plateau.

set-02-A-041.source: Physiology.html (thatboy) Q44, past question not in the original sets

M01-Q1.originalExplanation: Impaired venous drainage raises capillary pressure and promotes movement of fluid from capillaries into interstitial tissue. Why not the alternatives: Higher plasma oncotic pressure or stronger lymphatic removal would oppose fluid accumulation.

M01-Q2.originalExplanation: The flare of the triple response is produced by an antidromic axon reflex that dilates vessels around the stimulated region. Why not the alternatives: The wheal reflects increased local permeability, whereas the flare is spreading arteriolar vasodilation.

M01-Q3.originalExplanation: As cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure, the brachial artery is open throughout the cardiac cycle and the characteristic Korotkoff sounds generally disappear. Why not the alternatives: The first appearance of sound usually marks systolic rather than diastolic pressure.

M01-Q4.originalExplanation: Reduced medullary perfusion causes a powerful sympathetic rise in systemic pressure. The resulting arterial hypertension stimulates baroreceptors, producing reflex bradycardia. Why not the alternatives: The raised pressure is a compensatory response to brainstem ischemia; bradycardia is secondary to the baroreflex.

M01-Q5.originalExplanation: Tight junctions in cerebral capillary endothelium restrict movement between cells; astrocytes support barrier function. Not B: The choroid plexus forms a separate blood–CSF barrier. Not C: Loose venular junctions would not account for selective restriction. Not D: Astrocytes help maintain the barrier but are not the main sealed endothelial layer.

M01-Q6.originalExplanation: The SA node has the highest normal intrinsic pacemaker rate. Its impulses reach subsidiary pacemakers before those slower sites discharge. Why not the alternatives: Blood supply, contraction strength and ventricular conduction speed do not set the normal pacemaker hierarchy. Other conducting tissues also show automaticity.

M01-Q7.originalExplanation: The ECG measures electrical potentials. A larger recorded deflection may reflect electrical orientation or amplitude; it does not directly quantify mechanical stroke volume. Not A: Venous return is a haemodynamic variable not directly measured by the tracing. Not B: Duration is measured horizontally on ECG paper, not from complex height. Not C: A surface ECG records electrical potential rather than ventricular pressure.

M01-Q8.originalExplanation: During left ventricular systole, high intramyocardial pressure compresses coronary vessels, especially in the subendocardium. Relaxation during diastole permits better perfusion. Why not the alternatives: Coronary arterial openings remain connected to the aorta; the critical factor is compression by contracting myocardium.

M01-Q9.originalExplanation: An upward shift of the Frank-Starling curve indicates greater stroke volume at the same preload, consistent with increased contractility. Why not the alternatives: The comparison holds end-diastolic volume constant, so increased preload is not the explanation; reduced calcium response would tend to reduce contractility.

M01-Q10.originalExplanation: The lecture states that lung-inflation afferents travel in the vagus and can inhibit the vasomotor centre, lowering vascular tone and pressure. Not B: The carotid sinus is a stretch receptor, and the described effect is dilation. Not C: This is a lung-inflation input rather than an atrial filling response. Not D: The named afferent pathway is vagal and its effect is depressor.

M01-Q11.originalExplanation: Lung expansion and increased alveolar oxygen reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, raising pulmonary blood flow. Loss of the placenta simultaneously tends to raise systemic vascular resistance. Why not the alternatives: The first breaths promote pulmonary vasodilation, not vasoconstriction.

M01-Q12.originalExplanation: The aortic valve opens once left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, ending isovolumetric contraction and beginning ventricular ejection. The valve opens because the pressure gradient reverses, not simply because the ventricle contracts. Why not the alternatives: When aortic pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, the aortic valve remains closed. Left atrial and pulmonary arterial pressures do not determine its opening.

M01-Q13.originalExplanation: Fluid recruited from tissues or given intravenously restores volume before red-cell and protein mass recover, producing dilution. Not A: New red-cell production raises rather than lowers haemoglobin mass. Not B: Venoconstriction redistributes blood rather than removing haemoglobin. Not D: Renal filtration is generally depressed during acute severe shock.

M01-Q14.originalExplanation: The aqueduct links the third to the fourth ventricle. Obstruction causes CSF to accumulate upstream in the third and lateral ventricles. Why not the alternatives: The fourth ventricle lies downstream of the aqueduct and is not the primary site of enlargement in an isolated aqueduct blockage.

M01-Q15.originalExplanation: The long action potential and absolute refractory period prevent rapid re-excitation and mechanical summation into tetanus. Not A: Cardiac cells repeatedly generate action potentials. Not B: Calcium channels are essential for the cardiac plateau. Not C: Cardiac muscle contains actin and myosin.

M01-Q16.originalExplanation: A repolarisation wave has the opposite electrical sign to depolarisation; ventricular repolarisation also progresses in the reverse order, producing a T wave often concordant with QRS. Not A: Reversed direction without the polarity reversal would also favour opposite deflections. Not C: Depolarisation and repolarisation do not have the same electrical polarity. Not D: Opposite polarity without reversed direction would favour opposite QRS/T deflections.

M01-Q17.originalExplanation: Cerebral perfusion pressure is approximately MAP - ICP when ICP is the effective downstream pressure: 95 - 15 = 80 mmHg. Why not the alternatives: Perfusion pressure is a difference between driving and downstream pressures; it is not the MAP alone.

M01-Q18.originalExplanation: The mitral valve is closed because ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure. The aortic valve remains closed because ventricular pressure is still below aortic pressure. Rising pressure with both valves closed indicates isovolumetric contraction. Why not the alternatives: Ejection requires ventricular pressure above aortic pressure, while filling requires ventricular pressure below left atrial pressure.

M01-Q19.originalExplanation: During the occlusion, tissue oxygen delivery falls and local vasodilatory signals build up. When flow resumes, dilated resistance vessels produce transient reactive hyperaemia. Why not the alternatives: Reactive hyperaemia is a temporary local response to preceding flow interruption.

M01-Q20.originalExplanation: RAAS initially supports blood pressure, but prolonged salt and water retention increases filling pressures and oedema. Not A: Aldosterone promotes sodium retention rather than loss. Not B: RAAS tends to expand, not deplete, extracellular volume. Not D: Angiotensin II supports rather than blocks vasoconstriction.

M01-Q21.originalExplanation: Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius. Halving radius therefore increases resistance by 2^4 = 16 times. Why not the alternatives: The fourth-power dependence is stronger than a linear, square or cubic change.

M01-Q22.originalExplanation: The depressor area normally inhibits the pressor area; removing this brake permits more sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity. Not A: Disinhibition would increase, not decrease, pressor drive. Not B: A selective loss of pressor inhibition does not primarily increase vagal output. Not D: Local tissue metabolism is not directly abolished by this lesion.

M01-Q23.originalExplanation: Blood loss reduces circulating volume and venous return, which reduces preload and stroke volume. Reflex vasoconstriction may defend pressure but cannot automatically restore lost flow. Why not the alternatives: Loss of circulating volume does not directly raise preload or stroke volume.

M01-Q24.originalExplanation: SERCA normally resequesters calcium into the SR; inhibiting it prolongs the cytosolic calcium transient and slows relaxation. Not B: SERCA inhibition does not directly abolish membrane L-type channels. Not C: Less reuptake prolongs rather than shortens the cytosolic transient. Not D: Calcium removal becomes slower, not faster.

M01-Q25.originalExplanation: The horizontal duration is 4.5 × 0.04 = 0.18 s. This lies within the 0.12–0.20 s interval given in the lecture. Not A: This is not the product of 4.5 and 0.04 s. Not B: This incorrectly assigns 0.20 s to each small square. Not C: This incorrectly halves the duration obtained from 4.5 small squares.

M01-Q26.originalExplanation: Leakage from the dural puncture can reduce CSF pressure and cause a characteristic postural headache. Not A: The foramina are far from the lumbar puncture site. Not C: Production does not normally surge to cause this symptom. Not D: BBB disruption is not the usual cause of post-lumbar-puncture headache.

M01-Q27.originalExplanation: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, often prolonging right ventricular ejection and delaying P2 relative to A2. Why not the alternatives: S2 reflects semilunar valve closure, not AV valve opening or closure.

M01-Q28.originalExplanation: Poor left ventricular output raises pressure upstream in the left atrium and pulmonary veins. Higher pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes filtration and pulmonary oedema. Why not the alternatives: Fluid filtration increases with raised hydrostatic pressure; higher oncotic pressure would tend to oppose it.

M01-Q29.originalExplanation: The atrial stretch (Bainbridge) reflex can increase heart rate when venous return and atrial filling rise. It is distinct from the arterial baroreceptor response to elevated blood pressure. Why not the alternatives: Atrial distension can elicit reflex tachycardia without requiring arterial hypotension. The infusion increases rather than reduces venous return.

M01-Q30.originalExplanation: Greater afterload makes ventricular ejection more difficult. Before compensatory adjustments, end-systolic volume tends to increase and stroke volume decreases. Why not the alternatives: Aortic recoil, filling and AV conduction are not the mechanisms determining the first-beat afterload response.

M01-Q31.originalExplanation: The Circle of Willis provides proximal connections, but distal cerebral arterial territories have limited functional anastomoses. Not B: Basilar inflow does not directly replace all distal arterial territories. Not C: Distal vessels are not completely interconnected. Not D: Veins drain blood and cannot substitute for oxygenated arterial supply.

M01-Q32.originalExplanation: Ventricular ischaemia or hypoxia can disturb membrane potentials and cause ST elevation or depression, so the segment is useful in recognising myocardial injury patterns. Not A: Atrial depolarisation is the P wave and normally precedes ST. Not B: ST displacement is an electrical finding, not the normal marker of valve closure. Not C: Preload is a filling variable and does not directly set ST height.

M01-Q33.originalExplanation: Arterial-mixed venous oxygen content difference = 200 - 130 = 70 mL/L. Cardiac output = 280 mL/min divided by 70 mL/L = 4 L/min. Why not the alternatives: The Fick method divides oxygen consumption by the oxygen content difference, not by either concentration alone.

M01-Q34.originalExplanation: The myogenic response is the smooth muscle reacting to stretch itself: more stretch → more contraction. Responses driven by O₂, CO₂, H⁺, lactate or other chemicals are metabolic. Not A: Low oxygen is a metabolic signal for dilation. Not B: Lactate accumulation is a metabolic signal for dilation. Not D: Metabolite washout belongs to metabolic autoregulation.

M01-Q35.originalExplanation: The T wave reflects the slower process of ventricular repolarisation, while QRS represents rapid ventricular depolarisation through the conduction system. Not A: The T wave is still an electrical event, not the force of contraction. Not C: Atrial and ventricular depolarisation are represented mainly by P and QRS. Not D: The statement reverses the usual relative time courses.

M01-Q36.originalExplanation: Pulse pressure = 120 - 75 = 45 mmHg. MAP is approximately diastolic pressure + one-third of pulse pressure = 75 + 15 = 90 mmHg. Why not the alternatives: MAP is not the simple arithmetic midpoint; diastole usually occupies more time at rest.

M01-Q37.originalExplanation: Higher sinusoidal hydrostatic pressure increases fluid filtration and hepatic lymph formation; excess can enter the peritoneal cavity. Not B: Improved lymphatic clearance would tend to oppose accumulation. Not C: Oxygen tension is not the main Starling-force mechanism. Not D: Higher plasma oncotic pressure would oppose outward fluid filtration.

M01-Q38.originalExplanation: Micturition syncope is fainting associated with urination, often after rising at night, due to a reflex pressure fall. Not A: Carotid sinus syncope requires stimulation of a sensitive carotid region. Not B: There is no evidence of infection-related shock in the stem. Not D: Normal standing to urinate is not high positive acceleration.

M01-Q39.originalExplanation: Anaemia lowers viscosity and may increase cardiac output, raising the tendency to turbulent flow and a functional murmur. Not A: Anaemia decreases viscosity rather than increasing it. Not C: Conduction block is not the principal mechanism of flow murmurs. Not D: The murmur is not due to forced aortic valve closure.

M01-Q40.originalExplanation: At 25 mm/s, one small square = 0.04 s. Twenty squares = 0.8 s per beat, giving 60/0.8 = 75 beats/min. Equivalently, 1500/20 = 75 beats/min. Why not the alternatives: Heart rate depends on the R-R interval; the standard 25 mm/s conversion yields 1500 divided by small squares.

M01-Q41.originalExplanation: Gravity increases hydrostatic pressure and pooling in dependent veins. This reduces central venous return, initially lowering stroke volume and potentially cerebral perfusion. Why not the alternatives: Without compensation, standing does not drive leg blood centrally or raise head-level perfusion.

M01-Q42.originalExplanation: Gap junctions in intercalated discs permit ion current to spread from cell to cell, supporting a functional syncytium. Not B: Cardiac muscle does not require motor endplates for every contraction. Not C: Desmosomes provide mechanical attachment rather than electrical conductance. Not D: Connective tissue does not replace electrically coupled membranes.

M01-Q43.originalExplanation: HbF interacts less with 2,3-BPG, shifting its oxygen dissociation curve left and favouring oxygen uptake from maternal blood. Not A: Stronger 2,3-BPG binding would lower oxygen affinity. Not C: Fetal haemoglobin still contains iron-bearing haem groups. Not D: Oxygen binding is reversible, not permanent.

M01-Q44.originalExplanation: For approximately constant flow Q, a higher perfusion pressure requires a higher local resistance (Q = pressure difference / resistance). The plateau reflects autoregulatory adjustment. Why not the alternatives: Falling resistance alongside increasing pressure would increase, rather than stabilize, flow.

M01-Q45.originalExplanation: Stroke volume = 140 - 56 = 84 mL. Ejection fraction = (84/140) x 100 = 60%. Why not the alternatives: 84 mL is the stroke volume, not a percentage; 40% is the fraction remaining after systole.

M01-Q46.originalExplanation: Recruitment of additional pulmonary capillaries and distension of vessels increase the total flow capacity, limiting the rise in pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure. Why not the alternatives: Recruitment and distension expand, not reduce, pulmonary vascular capacity.

M01-Q47.originalExplanation: Sepsis can produce profound vasodilation and loss of vascular tone, lowering total peripheral resistance and effective perfusion pressure. This is distributive shock. Why not the alternatives: The defining event in this stem is widespread low resistance rather than haemorrhage, pump failure or obstruction.

M01-Q48.originalExplanation: For a given volume flow rate, average velocity equals flow divided by cross-sectional area. The enormous total capillary area produces low average velocity. Why not the alternatives: Flow continues in capillaries; the key comparison is total cross-sectional area, not the diameter of one capillary.

M01-Q49.originalExplanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies monitor oxygen, carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions, chiefly stimulating breathing. Not A: Atrial volume receptors principally detect filling and stretch. Not C: Arterial baroreceptors principally detect stretch. Not D: Cardiac nodes generate and conduct impulses rather than monitor arterial chemistry.

M01-Q50.originalExplanation: First-degree block delays conduction but retains a QRS after every P wave. In second-degree block, at least some atrial impulses fail to produce QRS complexes. Not A: Second-degree block is defined by intermittent failed conduction, not identical PR intervals. Not C: Both conditions can show P waves and QRS complexes on the trace. Not D: Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms indicate complete third-degree block.

M01-Q51.originalExplanation: Pressure work, which increases with afterload and myocardial wall tension, carries a high oxygen cost. Pumping the same volume against greater arterial pressure is more demanding. Why not the alternatives: The alternative changes reduce pressure load rather than increase it.

M01-Q52.originalExplanation: Less stretch of carotid and aortic baroreceptors reduces afferent firing. The medulla responds with increased sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic outflow. Why not the alternatives: Increased vagal activity would tend to slow the heart rather than compensate for falling pressure.

M01-Q53.originalExplanation: Heart failure includes states where output is maintained only at abnormally high filling pressures, causing congestion. Not B: High filling pressures can be evidence of dysfunction rather than normality. Not C: A near-normal output can be maintained at harmful filling pressures. Not D: Diastolic failure can occur with preserved ejection fraction.

M01-Q54.originalExplanation: Damage to lymphatic pathways reduces the return of interstitial fluid and proteins to the blood, producing lymphoedema. Why not the alternatives: Lymphoedema is caused by impaired lymph removal, not complete loss of arterial flow.

M01-Q55.originalExplanation: In aVF the left-foot electrode is positive and is compared with an average reference derived from the two arm electrodes. Not A: Chest electrodes make up V1–V6 and mainly examine the horizontal plane. Not C: Right arm versus left arm describes bipolar Lead I. Not D: The right-leg electrode is used for electrical noise reduction.

M01-Q56.originalExplanation: Low alveolar oxygen causes local pulmonary arteriolar constriction. This helps divert flow toward alveoli where oxygen uptake is more effective. Why not the alternatives: The pulmonary hypoxic response is opposite to the usual local hypoxic vasodilation in systemic tissues.

M01-Q57.originalExplanation: Reynolds number increases with velocity, density and diameter, and decreases with viscosity. Increased velocity therefore makes turbulence more likely. Why not the alternatives: Higher viscosity and smaller diameter generally lower Reynolds number when other variables are held constant.

M01-Q58.originalExplanation: More venous return increases ventricular filling and stretches cardiac fibres. On the ascending Frank-Starling relationship this raises force and stroke volume. Why not the alternatives: The Frank-Starling response links greater preload to greater output within physiological limits.

M01-Q59.originalExplanation: The x descent reflects atrial relaxation and downward tricuspid movement; the y descent follows tricuspid opening as blood empties rapidly. Not B: Left-heart valve events do not define these JVP descents. Not C: Atrial contraction creates the a wave. Not D: Both descents reflect right atrial pressure changes rather than the proposed events.

M01-Q60.originalExplanation: Atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve causes a sudden large rise in right atrial pressure, producing cannon or giant a waves. Why not the alternatives: The a wave reflects atrial contraction; the v wave mainly reflects atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed.

M02-Q1.originalExplanation: Inspiration decreases intrathoracic pressure and promotes a pressure gradient drawing blood from peripheral veins to the thorax. Not A: Venous valves do not all close in inspiration. Not B: Return is generally supported rather than abolished. Not D: Lower rather than higher thoracic pressure assists inflow.

M02-Q2.originalExplanation: Transmural pressure equals internal pressure minus surrounding tissue pressure; increasing the latter reduces the difference. Not A: A higher external pressure reduces, rather than widens, the difference. Not C: It equals internal pressure only when external pressure is zero. Not D: Transmural pressure depends on both internal and external pressure.

M02-Q3.originalExplanation: The placenta performs gas exchange before birth; fluid-filled fetal lungs have high resistance, favouring right-to-left shunts. Not A: Pulmonary resistance is high before aeration. Not B: The fetal left ventricle contributes significantly to systemic output. Not D: Umbilical arteries carry relatively deoxygenated blood toward placenta.

M02-Q4.originalExplanation: Elevated intrapericardial pressure limits end-diastolic filling and preload, reducing stroke volume. The restricted ventricular volume prevents an adequate Frank–Starling response. Not B: Tamponade reduces the ability of ventricles to expand. Not C: Venous return and effective filling become impaired. Not D: Valvular opening depends on pressure, but reduced preload is the central problem.

M02-Q5.originalExplanation: The increase is 10 beats/min × 70 mL/beat = 700 mL/min, or 0.70 L/min. Not A: 1.40 L/min doubles the actual change. Not C: 0.49 L/min does not follow from the given rate change. Not D: 0.80 L/min treats the extra beats as a larger volume.

M02-Q6.originalExplanation: Severe burns can cause plasma to leak through damaged skin while red cells remain, producing haemoconcentration and raised haematocrit. Not A: Erythropoiesis is much too slow to explain this early result. Not C: Plasma loss reduces rather than increases effective circulating volume. Not D: Selective red-cell destruction would tend to lower red-cell concentration.

M02-Q7.originalExplanation: Sympathetic drive raises heart rate and contractility while muscle pumping supports venous return, enabling higher cardiac output. Not A: Exercise generally increases rather than suppresses cardiac pumping. Not B: Reduced sympathetic drive does not explain exercise output. Not D: Vagal dominance would tend to slow the heart.

M02-Q8.originalExplanation: ADH promotes renal water conservation and has a vasoconstrictor action when its level is high. Not A: Prostacyclin dilates vessels and limits platelet aggregation. Not C: VIP is a vasodilator rather than a water-retaining hormone. Not D: ANP promotes sodium and water loss.

M02-Q9.originalExplanation: Systemic hypoxic tissues commonly dilate to improve supply, whereas low alveolar oxygen constricts adjacent pulmonary arterioles to improve ventilation–perfusion matching. Not A: Systemic tissues usually need increased flow in hypoxia. Not B: Oxygen tension influences both beds, but their dominant local responses differ. Not D: The response directions have been reversed.

M02-Q10.originalExplanation: Absorbed long-chain fats are packaged into chylomicrons and enter lacteals, reaching the blood via lymphatic drainage. Not A: Kidneys do not mediate initial intestinal fat absorption. Not B: Red cells normally remain in blood vessels. Not C: Most long-chain dietary fat reaches systemic blood through lymph rather than directly through portal blood.

M02-Q11.originalExplanation: A sustained systolic fall of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg within three minutes satisfies the criterion. Not A: The systolic threshold is met even when the diastolic threshold is not. Not B: The definition does not require both components to fall by 20 mmHg. Not D: The diagnostic threshold concerns the change, not a fixed final pressure.

M02-Q12.originalExplanation: In MAP ≈ CO × TPR, 0.80 × 1.25 = 1.00, so the changes cancel mathematically. Not A: The combined product does not fall by one quarter. Not B: That ignores the fall in cardiac output. Not C: That ignores the compensatory rise in resistance.

M02-Q13.originalExplanation: Extreme tachycardia shortens diastole, reduces filling and may decrease stroke volume enough to lower output. Not A: Contractility does not necessarily become zero. Not B: Diastole shortens markedly at high rates. Not C: Normal valves do not remain permanently open during extreme tachycardia.

M02-Q14.originalExplanation: Tachycardia increases cardiac oxygen demand and shortens diastole, reducing the time available for left ventricular coronary perfusion. Not A: The primary limitation is coronary supply through stenosed arteries during shortened diastole. Not B: An absent P wave is not the explanation of demand-related angina. Not D: Myocardial work and oxygen consumption generally rise with tachycardia.

M02-Q15.originalExplanation: The electrical depolarisation that activates cardiac muscle precedes its force development. P precedes atrial systole, and QRS precedes ventricular systole. Not A: The T wave reflects ventricular electrical recovery, after ventricular depolarisation. Not C: Pressure changes follow electrical activation and are not what skin ECG leads measure. Not D: This reverses the normal electrical-to-mechanical sequence.

M02-Q16.originalExplanation: The revised Starling model includes the glycocalyx and emphasises that sustained net filtration is normally cleared by lymphatics. Not A: Protein distributions can influence effective oncotic gradients. Not B: The classical arterial filtration–venous reabsorption picture overstates sustained reabsorption. Not C: Lymphatic return remains vital even at normal pressures.

M02-Q17.originalExplanation: Reduced blood ejected from the left heart impairs delivery to skeletal muscle and kidneys, causing fatigue and oliguria. Not B: Higher venous pressure does not directly improve GFR. Not C: The primary forward mechanism is reduced output, not pulmonary congestion. Not D: The syndrome involves reduced rather than excessive systemic delivery.

M02-Q18.originalExplanation: The dilators exist because flow was too low for demand. Once flow matches demand, they are washed away as fast as they are made, so the arterioles regain their tone. This negative feedback stops dilation running away. Not B: Restored delivery generally improves tissue oxygen availability. Not C: Sustained lactate accumulation would favour continued dilation. Not D: Vascular smooth muscle remains present and functional.

M02-Q19.originalExplanation: More red cells increase blood viscosity and consequently vascular resistance, raising the heart's workload. Not A: Higher viscosity raises resistance rather than lowering it. Not B: Lower viscosity does not follow from higher haematocrit. Not D: Both properties generally increase, not decrease.

M02-Q20.originalExplanation: With much of the ventricular myocardium at a similar depolarised membrane potential during the plateau, there is little net voltage difference to register. Not A: Ventricular repolarisation occurs during the following T wave, not before ST. Not B: Atrial and ventricular opposing depolarisations do not account for normal ST isoelectricity. Not D: By ST, the impulse has already activated the ventricles.

M02-Q21.originalExplanation: Low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure relative to plasma oncotic forces helps minimise filtration into air spaces. Not A: Plasma proteins contribute the inward oncotic force. Not B: Alveolar spaces normally contain little free fluid and protein. Not C: Pulmonary capillary pressure is much lower than systemic arterial pressure.

M02-Q22.originalExplanation: A higher capillary hydrostatic force favours filtration across the microvascular wall toward tissue. Raising venous pressure is one way to produce this hydrostatic change. Not A: The pressure favours outward, not reduced, filtration. Not C: Plasma oncotic pressure does not automatically increase. Not D: Lymphatic flow generally responds to excess tissue fluid rather than reversing.

M02-Q23.originalExplanation: Forward failure describes inadequate delivery to downstream tissues, whereas backward failure describes elevated pressure and congestion upstream of a failing chamber. Not A: Reduced flow and congestion, not excessive output, are the defining patterns. Not B: Either side can produce both forward and backward consequences. Not C: The two effects are reversed in this statement.

M02-Q24.originalExplanation: Working muscle uses ATP faster, and its breakdown products (adenosine, ADP, AMP) build up and dilate the local arterioles. Flow rises in proportion to how hard the tissue works, which is why the heart relies so heavily on this. Not B: Noradrenaline is a nerve transmitter that mainly constricts arterioles via α₁ receptors. Not C: Angiotensin II is a circulating constrictor, not a product of the muscle’s metabolism. Not D: Platelet serotonin constricts vessels, and it comes from platelets, not from the working muscle.

M02-Q25.originalExplanation: Venous return depends on the upstream systemic filling pressure relative to right atrial pressure and the resistance to venous return. Not A: Aortic-right ventricular systolic pressure is not the venous return driving gradient. Not B: Pulmonary venous pressure does not define systemic venous return. Not C: That difference is a pulse-pressure-related comparison.

M02-Q26.originalExplanation: Inadequate tissue oxygen delivery promotes anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis. The resulting acidemia can stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors and increase ventilation; reduced oxygen delivery alone is not equivalent to low arterial oxygen tension. Not A: Aerobic metabolism is limited by inadequate oxygen delivery. Not B: Chemoreceptor stimulation, rather than suppression, promotes respiration. Not D: Excess oxygen is not the initiating problem in shock.

M02-Q27.originalExplanation: Dividing daily production by total CSF volume gives 550/150 ≈ 3.7 turnovers each day. Not A: Two turnovers would require about 300 mL/day. Not B: One turnover would represent only about 150 mL/day. Not D: Six turnovers would correspond to around 900 mL/day.

M02-Q28.originalExplanation: The ventricle performs pressure–volume work as it ejects stroke volume against an arterial pressure load. Not A: Pacemaker electrical energy is not mechanical stroke work. Not B: Capillary recruitment affects supply, not the definition of work. Not C: Heart rate and surface area do not directly define mechanical work.

M02-Q29.originalExplanation: V1 is positioned in the fourth intercostal space at the right edge of the sternum; V2 lies at the left sternal edge at the same level. Not A: The anterior axillary position is used for V5. Not C: The midaxillary position is used for V6. Not D: The left midclavicular line in the fifth space is the usual site of V4.

M02-Q30.originalExplanation: Sympathetic arteriolar constriction can maintain arterial pressure despite reduced cardiac output and poor perfusion of some tissues. Not A: Shock is defined by inadequate tissue perfusion, not one pressure value. Not C: Flow can be redistributed away from skin and kidneys. Not D: Haemorrhage reduces venous return and usually lowers output.

M02-Q31.originalExplanation: Reduced albumin production lowers intravascular colloid oncotic pressure, allowing more net filtration and oedema. Not B: Lymphatic valve closure is not the universal mechanism. Not C: Advanced liver disease commonly reduces albumin synthesis. Not D: Plasma protein concentration is decreased, not increased.

M02-Q32.originalExplanation: Einthoven’s law is V(II) = V(I) + V(III). Therefore +0.4 + (−0.2) = +0.2 mV at the same instant. Not A: Lead II is obtained by combining the two measured limb-lead voltages. Not B: The negative sign of Lead III must be retained in the sum. Not C: This reverses the sign of the result rather than adding the signed voltages.

M02-Q33.originalExplanation: Active hyperaemia is the rise in flow while a tissue is working: its metabolites dilate the arterioles for as long as activity continues. Reactive hyperaemia is the surge after a blockage is released. Not B: The flow rises above baseline rather than staying constant. Not C: The increase originates largely from local demand, not a pressure-rise baroreflex. Not D: Reactive hyperaemia is a surge after an obstruction ends.

M02-Q34.originalExplanation: Aortic stenosis accelerates blood through a narrow outlet during systole, causing a turbulent ejection murmur. Not A: The aortic valve opens when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure in systole. Not B: Laminar flow through normal valves ordinarily produces no such murmur. Not C: Mitral regurgitation usually occurs during systole, not diastole.

M02-Q35.originalExplanation: Increased local CO₂ and H⁺ cause cerebral arteriolar vasodilation, improving blood delivery to metabolically active tissue. Not B: Isolated venular constriction does not explain metabolic regulation of cerebral arteriolar inflow. Not C: Constriction would reduce flow to the region that needs more oxygen. Not D: Capillary closure would worsen rather than correct the local supply-demand mismatch.

M02-Q36.originalExplanation: A lead is a directional electrical view. The normal mean ventricular depolarisation vector points generally towards Lead II and away from aVR. Not A: Lead orientation does not change the sequence of atrial and ventricular activation. Not B: Both QRS complexes represent ventricular depolarisation, despite opposite polarity. Not D: Both leads sample the electrical activity of the same heartbeat.

M02-Q37.originalExplanation: The ejection phase has an initial rapid phase followed by reduced ejection as the pressure and flow relationship changes. Not A: Ejection occurs during ventricular systole, before relaxation. Not C: Ejection rate declines rather than remaining uniform. Not D: The pattern is the reverse of the usual ejection phases.

M02-Q38.originalExplanation: Anaphylaxis releases mediators including histamine that widen vessels and increase capillary leakage, reducing effective perfusion. Not A: Anaphylaxis typically causes dilation and increased leak. Not C: Occult bleeding is not the primary allergic vascular mechanism. Not D: Higher pump performance would not explain the sudden widespread leakage.

M02-Q39.originalExplanation: When hypoxic constriction affects much of the lung, cumulative resistance rises and pulmonary arterial pressure can increase. Not B: Recruitment is a different response that lowers resistance. Not C: The lecture explicitly associates hypoxia with pulmonary vasoconstriction. Not D: Lung flow generally continues but faces increased resistance.

M02-Q40.originalExplanation: Early right ventricular contraction can bulge the shut tricuspid valve toward the right atrium, contributing to the c wave. Not A: Right atrial systole generates the a wave. Not C: Venous filling behind a closed tricuspid valve makes the v wave. Not D: Rapid atrial emptying contributes to the y descent.

M02-Q41.originalExplanation: With no nerve input the SA node fires at about 100 beats/min. At rest the vagus releases acetylcholine continuously (vagal tone), holding the rate down to about 60–80. Blocking the vagus, for example with atropine, lets the rate rise. Not A: Sympathetic activity usually increases SA nodal firing. Not B: Atrial conduction is not the main cause of the slower intrinsic SA pacemaker rate. Not D: The isolated rate shows the pacemaker is capable of firing faster.

M02-Q42.originalExplanation: Severe myocardial, neural and microvascular damage may prevent recovery even after the original blood-volume loss has been corrected. Not A: Postural hypotension should depend on standing and impaired compensation. Not B: Compensated shock should retain useful mechanisms for pressure support. Not C: An uncomplicated faint generally improves rapidly when lying flat.

M02-Q43.originalExplanation: More interstitial protein increases interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, tending to pull fluid outward from the capillary and increase filtration. Not A: Plasma protein concentration is held constant; the changed force is interstitial. Not B: Increased proteins outside the capillary attract rather than remove interstitial water. Not C: A change in interstitial protein does not directly lower capillary pressure.

M02-Q44.originalExplanation: Complete (third-degree) block produces atrioventricular dissociation: atria and ventricles follow independent rhythms without consistent P-to-QRS conduction. Not B: Normal sinus rhythm has a consistent P wave preceding each conducted QRS. Not C: First-degree block maintains a consistent P-to-QRS relationship with prolonged PR. Not D: Second-degree block has intermittent failure, rather than complete independence.

M02-Q45.originalExplanation: For a cylinder, wall tension T = P × r. With equal transmural pressure, the vessel with twice the radius needs twice the tension. This is why a capillary’s tiny radius lets a one-cell wall withstand blood pressure. Not A: A fourfold difference does not follow the linear radius relation. Not B: Equal pressure alone does not make tension equal. Not D: Half the tension would apply to half the radius.

M02-Q46.originalExplanation: The AV delay separates atrial and ventricular activation so atrial systole can augment ventricular filling before ventricular systole. Not B: Normal impulses subsequently travel through His and Purkinje fibres. Not C: The sequence is atrial activation before ventricular activation. Not D: The aortic valve remains closed during ordinary atrial systole.

M02-Q47.originalExplanation: Sympathetic constriction reduces skin flow to preserve perfusion for vital organs, producing pallor and coolness. Not B: Loss of sympathetic tone would usually warm and flush skin. Not C: Higher cutaneous blood volume tends to increase redness. Not D: The primary response is systemic compensation, not skin warming.

M02-Q48.originalExplanation: Once arterioles are fully dilated, they cannot reduce resistance further, so flow decreases as pressure falls. Not A: Venous vessels do not replace arterioles as the chief resistance site. Not C: A downward slope does not mean perfusion pressure is zero. Not D: Maximal constriction occurs in response to rising pressure, not very low pressure.

M02-Q49.originalExplanation: Slow inward calcium current and outward potassium current maintain the prolonged plateau before repolarisation. Not A: Calcium entry contributes substantially to phase 2. Not C: Fast sodium influx creates phase 0, not the sustained plateau. Not D: Unopposed potassium efflux would favour repolarisation.

M02-Q50.originalExplanation: With capillary entry relatively open but venular outflow restricted, blood stagnates and local capillary pressure rises, driving fluid into the interstitium. Not B: Greater drainage would reduce rather than increase local stagnation. Not C: Lower entry with free outflow would not cause the described stasis. Not D: Both reduced entry and improved drainage favour lower capillary pressure.

M02-Q51.originalExplanation: Centrilobular cells receive blood after it has travelled from portal triads, making them less oxygenated and vulnerable. Not A: Oxygenated hepatic arterial inflow enters near the portal triads. Not B: Centrilobular hepatocytes remain within the sinusoidal perfusion system. Not C: Blood oxygen content generally falls as it traverses sinusoids.

M02-Q52.originalExplanation: Trigger calcium opens ryanodine receptors, releasing stored calcium in calcium-induced calcium release. This amplifies the small trigger signal into a large intracellular calcium release. Not B: Ryanodine receptors open rather than close in this mechanism. Not C: SERCA pumps calcium back into the SR during relaxation. Not D: Calcium binds troponin C; ATP hydrolysis occurs in cross-bridge cycling.

M02-Q53.originalExplanation: The limb leads provide frontal-plane views, while the precordial leads examine the same heart from different points around the horizontal plane. Not A: Chest leads, like limb leads, still record surface electrical potentials. Not B: Both sets of leads record combined cardiac electrical events. Not C: Frontal and horizontal views complement rather than replace one another.

M02-Q54.originalExplanation: Lower afferent firing releases the pressor area and reduces vagal inhibition, raising heart rate, contractility and vascular tone. Not A: Greater vagal drive would slow the heart, while low return worsens output. Not B: That combination is appropriate to a rise in pressure. Not D: Sympathetic withdrawal and venous storage would further lower pressure.

M02-Q55.originalExplanation: Viscous drag slows flow near the wall; a parabolic velocity profile has its greatest velocity near the centre. Not A: The no-slip boundary makes velocity near the wall approach zero. Not C: Laminar flow has a radial velocity gradient. Not D: The plasma layer adjacent to the wall is not the maximum-velocity region.

M02-Q56.originalExplanation: Doubling paper speed doubles the horizontal distance covered during a fixed physiological interval. A 0.16-s PR interval spans 8 mm at 50 mm/s versus 4 mm at 25 mm/s. Not B: The number of squares changes because time calibration depends on paper speed. Not C: A faster recording speed spreads the same time over more paper, not less. Not D: Vertical squares measure voltage and are unaffected by horizontal paper speed.

M02-Q57.originalExplanation: Right ventricular backward failure elevates right atrial and systemic venous pressures, causing jugular distension, hepatic congestion and dependent oedema. Not B: Isolated pulmonary venous congestion principally reflects left-sided failure. Not C: Higher systemic venous pressure promotes, rather than reduces, filtration. Not D: Right-sided backward failure increases rather than decreases venous pressure.

M02-Q58.originalExplanation: S4 is associated with late-diastolic atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, which causes low-frequency vibrations. Not A: Systolic ejection turbulence describes a murmur, not S4. Not B: Pulmonary valve opening occurs in systole. Not D: Rapid passive filling is associated with S3 rather than S4.

M02-Q59.originalExplanation: Glucose crosses the BBB through transporters such as GLUT1; its entry does not require insulin. Not A: Cerebral glucose transport is largely insulin independent. Not C: Endothelial tight junctions block most paracellular solutes. Not D: Protein leakage is limited by the barrier.

M02-Q60.originalExplanation: An undersized cuff transmits pressure poorly around a large arm and commonly overestimates measured pressure. Not A: Both systolic and diastolic measurements may be distorted. Not B: Cuff size materially affects readings. Not C: A small cuff usually overestimates rather than underestimates BP.

M03-Q1.originalExplanation: The SA node initiates impulses that reach the AV node, traverse the His–bundle branches and Purkinje system, then depolarise ventricles. Not A: The SA node normally initiates atrial excitation. Not C: Purkinje fibres come after the AV–His pathway. Not D: Ventricular Purkinje fibres conduct after, not before, atrial activation.

M03-Q2.originalExplanation: The lecture describes a transient white reaction due to constriction; it is distinct from the classical red–flare–wheal response. Not B: The red line is a separate vasodilator response. Not C: Flare is surrounding redness from arteriolar dilation. Not D: Wheal is raised local oedema from permeability.

M03-Q3.originalExplanation: Medullary ischaemia first raises sympathetic pressure; arterial baroreceptors then increase vagal drive and slow the heart. Not A: β₁ stimulation would usually accelerate, not slow, the heart. Not B: Atrial volume receptors respond chiefly to filling, not this sequence. Not D: Cardiac autonomic signalling remains central to the response.

M03-Q4.originalExplanation: Sympathetic venoconstriction reduces the capacity of the venous reservoir and shifts stored blood toward the heart, supporting venous return and end-diastolic filling. Not B: Venodilation generally increases peripheral capacitance and pooling. Not C: Venoconstriction redistributes existing blood rather than rapidly generating plasma. Not D: Systemic arterioles have no valves that close with sympathetic stimulation.

M03-Q5.originalExplanation: Positive g causes leg pooling and reduced pressure at eye level, so retinal perfusion can fail before cerebral consciousness. Not B: Pressure at eye level decreases during positive g. Not C: The mechanism is reduced eye-level arterial perfusion, not an inevitable ICP excess. Not D: Headward blood movement occurs during negative g.

M03-Q6.originalExplanation: Prolonged severe ischaemia can cause irreversible myocardial cell death; transient angina does not necessarily cause necrosis. Not A: Transient angina ordinarily reflects reversible myocardial ischaemia. Not B: Stable angina may result from fixed stenosis without rupture. Not C: Infarction can occur across a range of heart rates.

M03-Q7.originalExplanation: Greater downstream resistance reduces diastolic runoff from the elastic arterial reservoir; at unchanged compliance, aortic pressure falls more slowly. Not A: Higher resistance slows forward runoff but does not reverse normal arterial flow. Not B: Diastolic decay depends in part on resistance and arterial compliance. Not D: Greater resistance normally reduces runoff rather than increasing it.

M03-Q8.originalExplanation: Acute whole-blood loss removes red cells and plasma proportionately, so concentration may remain unchanged before fluid replacement. Not A: Early dilution has not yet occurred in this scenario. Not C: Erythropoiesis takes days to weeks, not minutes. Not D: Red-cell mass falls with whole-blood loss.

M03-Q9.originalExplanation: Venodilation increases capacitance, allowing veins to hold more blood and tending to reduce venous return. Not A: Arteriolar tone is the principal determinant of peripheral resistance. Not C: Capillaries are not the main contractile vessels. Not D: Venoconstriction, not venodilation, mobilises stored blood.

M03-Q10.originalExplanation: The lecture describes phosphodiesterase inhibition by xanthines, which slows cAMP breakdown; increased cAMP-dependent signalling can enhance myocardial calcium handling and contractility. Not A: Reducing calcium entry would tend to depress rather than enhance contraction. Not B: Faster cAMP degradation would reduce this positive inotropic pathway. Not D: Blocking beta-1 signalling would generally reduce adrenergic inotropy.

M03-Q11.originalExplanation: Increased pulmonary venous return elevates left atrial pressure while loss of placental venous return reduces right-sided filling, pressing the flap closed. Not A: Pulmonary resistance falls with first breaths. Not B: Clamping removes rather than increases umbilical venous return. Not D: Right atrial dominance normally supports fetal shunting, not closure.

M03-Q12.originalExplanation: β₂ effects can favour dilation in skeletal muscle, while α₁ effects cause constriction in many skin and gut vessels. Not A: The difference is due mainly to receptor distribution rather than selective circulating delivery. Not B: Plasma volume differences do not explain opposite receptor responses. Not C: Muscle vessels respond because they possess adrenergic receptors.

M03-Q13.originalExplanation: S3 occurs during rapid early-diastolic ventricular filling, as blood entering the chamber causes vibrations. Not A: Aortic valve opening occurs during ventricular systole. Not C: Isovolumetric contraction occurs near S1. Not D: Atrial depolarisation precedes the atrial contribution later in diastole.

M03-Q14.originalExplanation: The rapid baroreflex stabilizes pressure within seconds, while the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system supports longer-term pressure and volume. Not B: Aldosterone supports sodium retention rather than its suppression. Not C: Loss of arteriolar responsiveness would worsen orthostatic control. Not D: Baroreflexes remain available during sustained standing.

M03-Q15.originalExplanation: Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when CSF reaches subarachnoid space but reabsorption is impaired. The ventricular pathway remains open, so the defect is in absorption rather than transit. Not B: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus results from blocked ventricular drainage. Not C: Haemorrhage may contribute to hydrocephalus but is not the classification described. Not D: Aqueductal stenosis is a specific obstruction.

M03-Q16.originalExplanation: Elastic arteries stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing pulsatile ejection into continuous downstream flow. Not A: Capillaries lack the pumping muscle required to drive systemic flow. Not B: Respiratory movement mainly assists venous return. Not C: Venous valves prevent backflow but do not create aortic pressure.

M03-Q17.originalExplanation: Parasympathetic acetylcholine acts at muscarinic M₂ receptors to slow both SA nodal firing and AV nodal conduction. Not A: β₁ activation describes sympathetic, not vagal, stimulation. Not B: The major cardiac pacemaker effect is not mediated by α₁. Not C: AV conduction is slowed rather than accelerated by vagal action.

M03-Q18.originalExplanation: Only the component of the electrical vector along the lead axis contributes strongly to the deflection; a near-perpendicular vector has a small projection. Not A: Vector orientation changes amplitude and polarity, not necessarily conduction duration. Not C: A strongly upright deflection needs a substantial vector component towards the positive pole. Not D: A strongly downward deflection needs a substantial vector component away from the positive pole.

M03-Q19.originalExplanation: Tricuspid regurgitation sends systolic flow back into the right atrium and systemic veins, producing a large v or fused c-v wave. Not A: The x descent may be blunted rather than unusually enlarged. Not C: The a wave reflects atrial contraction and is not the characteristic regurgitant finding. Not D: The y descent is an emptying phase and does not represent systolic backflow.

M03-Q20.originalExplanation: The splanchnic bed is a large blood reservoir; vasoconstriction redirects perfusion and recruits stored blood toward central circulation. Not B: Extraction is not necessarily complete. Not C: Mucosal flow may decrease, risking ischaemia. Not D: Severe or prolonged constriction can contribute to intestinal injury.

M03-Q21.originalExplanation: Coronary ischaemia depresses myocardial contractility, lowering output and pressure, which further compromises myocardial blood supply. Not A: Lower resistance cannot fully resolve a collapsing pump. Not B: Ischaemia reduces rather than increases available myocardial ATP. Not C: Lower cardiac output tends to worsen coronary perfusion, not restore it.

M03-Q22.originalExplanation: Higher right atrial pressure opposes venous return and transmits backward into systemic veins, causing congestion. Not A: Higher right atrial pressure reduces the upstream-to-atrial gradient. Not B: Elevated atrial pressure tends to increase congestion. Not D: JVP often becomes elevated rather than disappearing.

M03-Q23.originalExplanation: The lecture describes a U wave, when seen after T, as the final remnants of ventricular repolarisation. Its precise physiological origin is uncertain. Not A: Atrial depolarisation is the P wave preceding QRS. Not C: Rapid ventricular depolarisation is represented by QRS, not U. Not D: The ventricular plateau is associated with the ST segment.

M03-Q24.originalExplanation: A more horizontal posture decreases the vertical distance over which acceleration reduces pressure toward the head and brain. Not A: Increasing the vertical distance would worsen the gradient. Not C: Greater dependent filtration would not protect brain perfusion. Not D: Enhanced ankle pooling would reduce central venous return.

M03-Q25.originalExplanation: Complete AV block prevents atrial impulses from reaching ventricles; a slower escape pacemaker may maintain ventricular rhythm. Not B: The lungs do not provide an alternative physiological conduction path. Not C: Valves do not propagate cardiac electrical impulses. Not D: Faster atrial activity alone cannot restore complete AV conduction.

M03-Q26.originalExplanation: Small diffusible gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the endothelial membrane relatively easily. Not A: Albumin is a large protein with restricted passage. Not C: Protein binding reduces free diffusion across the BBB. Not D: Large immunoglobulins do not easily cross intact endothelial tight junctions.

M03-Q27.originalExplanation: Active muscle generates enough vasodilator metabolites to oppose sympathetic constriction, redirecting blood to the tissue that needs it. Not B: Constriction does not raise flow equally across every organ. Not C: Sympathetic activity often remains elevated; metabolites oppose its constrictor effect locally. Not D: Metabolites in working muscle predominantly dilate its arterioles.

M03-Q28.originalExplanation: Proteinuria reduces circulating albumin and its inward oncotic force, favouring movement of fluid into interstitium. Not A: Viscosity is not the principal mechanism of protein-loss oedema. Not B: Albumin loss lowers oncotic pressure. Not D: Capillary permeability elsewhere need not decrease.

M03-Q29.originalExplanation: Sympatholytic drugs blunt reflex arteriolar and venous constriction, so the circulation cannot adequately oppose blood pooling and falling arterial pressure on standing. Not B: Walking uses a mechanical muscle pump, not this autonomic drug pathway. Not C: Cerebral metabolic vasodilatation is not directly a sympathetic vasoconstrictor response. Not D: Venous valve directionality is mechanical and not directly abolished by sympatholytic drugs.

M03-Q30.originalExplanation: Sympathetic stimulation raises cardiac work and oxygen demand; local metabolites then increase coronary perfusion despite competing vasomotor effects. Not A: Coronary flow is not increased by closing the arterioles. Not B: Greater work increases, not reduces, ATP consumption. Not D: Reduced contraction is not the expected beta-mediated cardiac response.

M03-Q31.originalExplanation: A mixed venous sample from pulmonary artery reflects oxygen after extraction across the whole body. Not A: One local vein does not represent average whole-body extraction. Not B: Active muscle has unusually high local extraction and can misrepresent the body. Not D: Arterial blood provides the other concentration in the equation.

M03-Q32.originalExplanation: When pressure stays high for days, the baroreceptors reset and treat the new level as normal, so they defend it instead of correcting it. Long-term pressure is set mainly by the kidneys’ control of salt and water. Not A: Unbounded sensitivity would strongly oppose the persistent rise. Not B: Sensory fibres do not become motor fibres. Not C: Resetting does not require loss of every afferent signal.

M03-Q33.originalExplanation: Atrial repolarisation occurs around the time of ventricular depolarisation; the much larger QRS electrical signal masks it on the surface trace. Not A: Atrial repolarisation does not need to await the beginning of ventricular diastole. Not B: Repolarisation does generate voltage differences, although the signal is small. Not C: That statement does not explain why the wave is not separately visible.

M03-Q34.originalExplanation: Severe hypoxia and acidosis impair myocardial function and are listed as causes of depressed inotropy. Not A: Catecholamines usually raise inotropy initially. Not C: Increased cytosolic calcium generally enhances contraction. Not D: Beta-1 activation generally enhances contractility.

M03-Q35.originalExplanation: Diastolic failure reflects impaired relaxation and stiff ventricular filling; the fraction of blood ejected can remain normal despite elevated filling pressures and reduced filling volume. Not A: Increased contractility is not the primary defect. Not C: SA-node dysfunction does not define diastolic heart failure. Not D: A stiff ventricle has reduced, not excessive, compliance.

M03-Q36.originalExplanation: A narrowed vessel may deliver adequate resting flow but cannot dilate enough to meet exercise demand, causing reversible ischaemia. Not A: Plaque does not disappear with exertion. Not B: Exercise raises myocardial work and oxygen requirements. Not C: Resting coronary flow may be sufficient despite reduced reserve.

M03-Q37.originalExplanation: Systemic venous return fills the right atrium during ventricular systole while the tricuspid valve remains closed, creating the v wave. Not B: Pulmonary valve closure is near S2. Not C: Atrial depolarisation precedes the a wave. Not D: The v wave is defined by right atrial filling rather than aortic ejection.

M03-Q38.originalExplanation: The pressor area sends excitatory fibres down to the sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord. More sympathetic output constricts arterioles and veins and speeds and strengthens the heart, so pressure rises. Not A: Carotid sinus fibres carry sensory information towards the medulla. Not B: Pressor-area activity does not require direct pacemaker inhibition. Not D: Inhibiting sympathetic neurons would tend to lower pressure.

M03-Q39.originalExplanation: A lead is an electrical viewpoint calculated from one or more electrode potentials, so ten physical contacts can generate twelve different standard recordings. Not A: The limb contacts remain in place during a standard recording. Not C: Routine twelve-lead ECG does not require intracardiac electrodes. Not D: All twelve are electrical leads; pressure sensors do not generate extra leads.

M03-Q40.originalExplanation: Rapid His–Purkinje conduction activates much of ventricular myocardium in a short time for synchronised pumping. Not A: The key AV delay occurs before the His–Purkinje network. Not B: Purkinje fibres primarily serve ventricles, not the atrial septum. Not C: Pulmonary valve closure occurs after ventricular ejection.

M03-Q41.originalExplanation: The arterial–venous difference changes by −30 minus −25, or −5 mmHg. Falling venous and intracranial pressures therefore help protect cerebral perfusion. Not A: That ignores the fall in cerebral venous pressure. Not B: The difference becomes slightly smaller, not larger. Not C: The changes cannot be added as two rises.

M03-Q42.originalExplanation: Six seconds is one tenth of a minute. Eleven QRS complexes over that span give an approximate average ventricular rate of 11 × 10 = 110 beats/min. Not A: This multiplies the QRS count by six, not by ten. Not C: A rate of 90 beats/min would correspond to nine complexes in six seconds. Not D: A rate of 100 beats/min would correspond to ten complexes in six seconds.

M03-Q43.originalExplanation: Beta-1 signalling raises cAMP and PKA activity, enhancing calcium entry and cycling for stronger contraction. Not A: Beta-1 stimulation raises, not lowers, cAMP. Not B: Vagal slowing is not the main ventricular inotropic pathway. Not D: Blocking release channels would reduce systolic calcium release.

M03-Q44.originalExplanation: Some bronchial venous return enters pulmonary veins, mixing a small amount of deoxygenated blood with oxygenated pulmonary venous blood. Not A: Not all bronchial venous blood returns only through systemic veins. Not B: Bronchial arteries arise from the systemic arterial circulation. Not C: Normal pulmonary blood passes through alveolar capillary networks.

M03-Q45.originalExplanation: Reduced right ventricular output limits pulmonary flow and subsequent return to the left atrium, compromising left-sided filling and delivery. Not A: The right heart cannot deliver excess flow when severely failing. Not C: Reduced pulmonary transit cannot raise systemic oxygen delivery. Not D: Less pulmonary venous return tends to decrease left-sided filling.

M03-Q46.originalExplanation: Semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic or pulmonary arterial pressure. The pressure reversal is the immediate mechanical trigger for valve opening. Not B: Atrial systole precedes isovolumetric contraction. Not C: Lower ventricular than aortic pressure holds the aortic valve closed. Not D: This pressure relation opens the AV valves during filling.

M03-Q47.originalExplanation: PR includes the P wave itself and conduction through atrial tissue, AV node and His–Purkinje system before QRS begins. AV nodal delay is only one component. Not A: Mechanical valve events are not boundaries of the PR interval. Not B: Ventricular repolarisation is represented by T and included in QT. Not C: End-QRS to start-T corresponds to the ST segment.

M03-Q48.originalExplanation: The lecture distinguishes the pressor response to short, sharp pain from depressor vasodilation and possible syncope with sustained pain. Not A: The directions of vascular changes are reversed in this option. Not C: Prolonged pain may produce hypotension rather than unbounded resistance. Not D: Short sharp pain can stimulate rather than inhibit pressor activity.

M03-Q49.originalExplanation: Higher aortic pressure can produce a louder aortic component (A2) of S2 because aortic valve closure is more forceful. Not B: Tricuspid closure contributes to S1, not A2. Not C: Mitral closure contributes to S1, not the aortic component of S2. Not D: Pulmonary resistance and right ventricular ejection primarily influence P2 timing.
